\documentclass[11pt,a4paper]{amsart}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amssymb,microtype}
\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}

\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
\newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}
\newcommand{\R}{\mathbb R}
\newcommand{\Z}{\mathbb Z}
\newcommand{\A}{\mathcal A}
\newcommand{\B}{\mathcal B}
\newcommand{\norm}[1]{\lVert#1\rVert}
\newcommand{\vol}{\operatorname{vol}}
\newcommand{\Lip}{\operatorname{Lip}}
\newcommand{\av}[1]{\langle#1\rangle}

\title{Symmetric floating bodies}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\begin{abstract}
We construct nonspherical, centrally symmetric, strictly convex bodies of
revolution in four dimensions that have real-analytic boundaries and float
in equilibrium in every orientation.
Their relative densities tend to an explicit number near $0.218294$ as the
bodies tend to the unit ball.
The construction starts from a finite-order expansion and uses an analytic
Newton iteration on closed sets of chord parameters whose relative measure
tends to one.
\end{abstract}
\maketitle

\section{The floating condition}

A homogeneous body of relative density $\rho\in(0,1)$ floats in equilibrium
in the direction $n$ if a hyperplane perpendicular to $n$ cuts off a portion
of volume $\rho\vol K$ whose centroid lies on the line through the centroid
of $K$ parallel to $n$ \cite{Ryabogin23}.
Ryabogin constructed nonspherical convex bodies with this property in every
orientation at density $1/2$ \cite{Ryabogin22}.
At that density, central symmetry forces a convex body to be a ball
\cite{Florentin}.
Wegner developed formal expansions for centrally symmetric bodies at other
densities \cite{Wegner}.
Here we obtain exact analytic bodies in $\R^4$.

Let $U_l(\cos x)=\sin((l+1)x)/\sin x$ and $Z_l=U_l/(l+1)$.
Set
\begin{equation}\label{constants}
 h=\frac1{\sqrt8},\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\frac78},\qquad
 a_* =\arccos h,\qquad V_0=\frac{\pi^2}{2},\qquad
 \rho_* =\frac{a_*}{\pi}-\frac{19\sqrt7}{96\pi}.
\end{equation}
Here $V_0=\vol B^4$ and
$\rho_*V_0=(4\pi/3)\int_h^1(1-u^2)^{3/2}\,du$.
For a periodic function $u=\sum_k u_ke^{ikx}$, write
$\norm{u}_r=\sum_k|u_k|e^{r|k|}$ and denote the resulting analytic Wiener
algebra by $\A_r$.
An estimate for a radial function in this norm refers to its restriction
$x\mapsto R(\cos x,\sin x,0,0)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{main}
There are nonspherical, origin-symmetric, strictly convex bodies of
revolution $K\subset\R^4$, of volume $V_0$, with real-analytic boundary,
which float in equilibrium in every orientation at a relative density
different from $1/2$.
They occur arbitrarily close to the unit ball and satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{asymptotics}
 R(\omega)=1+\varepsilon Z_4(\omega_1)+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad
 \rho=\rho_*-\frac{49\sqrt7}{1200\pi}\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2),
\end{equation}
where $\varepsilon>0$ is the degree-four coefficient of $R$ and the
remainders are bounded in a fixed $\A_r$, $r>0$.
More precisely, for every fixed $0<c_1<c_2$ and all sufficiently small
$t>0$, there is a closed set
$G_t\subset I_t=[a_*+c_1t,a_*+c_2t]$ with
$|G_t|/|I_t|\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$.
For each $a\in G_t$, a body as above has an analytic meridian
parametrization $\gamma$ in which the cutting chords join
$\gamma(x-a)$ to $\gamma(x+a)$, and
$a-a_*=(\sqrt7/50)\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
\end{theorem}

For an origin-symmetric convex body define
$V(n,d)=\vol\{z\in K:n\cdot z>d\}$ and
$J(n,d)=\int_K(n\cdot z-d)_+\,dz$.
For $0<\nu<\vol K$, the height $d(n)$ giving cap volume $\nu$ is unique.
Since $\partial_dJ=-V$, the function
$E(n)=J(n,d(n))+\nu d(n)$ satisfies
$DE(n)[e]=\int_{n\cdot z>d(n)}e\cdot z\,dz$ for $e\perp n$.
Consequently, $K$ floats in every orientation at density $\nu/\vol K$
if and only if $E$ is constant.

We shall use $\norm{uv}_r\le\norm u_r\norm v_r$, the isometry
$T_au(x)=u(x+a)$ for real $a$, and
$\norm{\partial_x^mu}_{r-\delta}\le m!\delta^{-m}\norm u_r$.
For a family on a closed set $G\subset I_t$, put
\begin{equation}\label{lipnorm}
 \norm u^{\Lip}_{r,t;G}
 =\sup_{a\in G}\norm{u(a)}_r
 +t\sup_{\substack{a,b\in G\\a\ne b}}
       \frac{\norm{u(a)-u(b)}_r}{|a-b|}.
\end{equation}
The second supremum is zero for a singleton.
Products obey the same algebra estimate in this norm.
All parameter estimates below concern these difference quotients on $G$.
In Fourier calculations, angle brackets denote the normalized average
over one period.

\section{Expansion at the ball}

Write $C_l^\lambda$ for the Gegenbauer polynomials defined by
$(1-2xz+z^2)^{-\lambda}=\sum_{l\ge0}C_l^\lambda(x)z^l$.
Let $C_h$ and $T_h$ be the spherical integral operators with kernels
$\mathbf1_{\{n\cdot\omega>h\}}$ and $(n\cdot\omega-h)_+$,
respectively, using the ordinary area measure on $S^3$.

\begin{lemma}\label{arithmetic}
For $l\ge2$, their multipliers are
\begin{equation}\label{multipliers}
 c_l(h)=\frac{8\pi(1-h^2)^{3/2}C_{l-1}^2(h)}{l(l+1)(l+2)},\qquad
 t_l(h)=\frac{32\pi(1-h^2)^{5/2}C_{l-2}^3(h)}
 {(l-1)l(l+1)(l+2)(l+3)}.
\end{equation}
At the value of $h$ in \eqref{constants}, $C_n^3(h)=0$ exactly when $n=2$.
There are positive constants $c,C,\tau_*$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{arithmeticbounds}
 |C_n^3(h)|\ge c(n+1)^2e^{-C\log^2(n+2)}\quad(n\ne2),\qquad
 |2\sin(ma_*)|\ge c(1+|m|)^{-\tau_*}\quad(m\ne0).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The Funk--Hecke formula gives
$t_l=4\pi\int_h^1(t-h)Z_l(t)\sqrt{1-t^2}\,dt$.
Two integrations using
$((1-t^2)^{\lambda+1/2}(C_l^\lambda)')'
=-l(l+2\lambda)(1-t^2)^{\lambda-1/2}C_l^\lambda$
and $(C_l^\lambda)'=2\lambda C_{l-1}^{\lambda+1}$ give
\eqref{multipliers} and $t_l'=-c_l$; these polynomial conventions agree
with \cite[Chapter 18]{DLMF}.

Put $\alpha=(1+i\sqrt7)/2$, $\beta=\overline\alpha$, $\Delta=i\sqrt7$,
$A_n=7n^2+45n+62$, $B_n=6n+18$, and $Q_n(X)=-A_n+B_nX$.
Partial fractions give
\begin{equation}\label{partialfractions}
 a_n=[z^n](1-z+2z^2)^{-3}
 =(\sqrt2)^nC_n^3(h)
 =\frac{\alpha^{n+3}Q_n(\beta)-\beta^{n+3}Q_n(\alpha)}{2\Delta^5}.
\end{equation}
Since $\alpha+\beta=1$, their principal ideals in $\Z[\alpha]$ are
coprime. Thus $a_n=0$ implies that $\alpha^{n+3}$ divides $Q_n(\alpha)$,
and taking norms gives $2^{n+3}\mid M(n)$, where
$M(n)=49n^4+588n^3+2569n^2+4830n+3376$.
Now $M(21)=16212772<2^{24}$ and
$M(n+1)/M(n)\le((n+1)/n)^4<2$ for $n\ge6$.
This excludes $n\ge21$.
For $0\le n\le20$, the successive values of $v_2(M(n))$ are
$4,2,7,5,3,2,3,5,5,2,4,7,3,2,3,10,4,2,5,5,3$.
Only $n=0,2$ meet the divisibility condition, and $a_0=1$, $a_2=0$.
These finite checks can also be made from
$(n+1)a_{n+1}=(n+3)a_n-(2n+10)a_{n-1}$, with $a_{-1}=0$, $a_0=1$.

For the estimates, set $\Gamma=\alpha/\beta=(-3+i\sqrt7)/4$ and
$\omega_n=Q_n(\beta)/Q_n(\alpha)$.
Both lie in a fixed quadratic field, have modulus one, and
$H(\omega_n)\le\frac12\log M(n)$, where $H$ is the absolute logarithmic
height. Indeed, $\omega_n$ and its conjugate are the roots of
$M(n)X^2-((2A_n-B_n)^2-2M(n))X+M(n)$.
We use the following consequence of the theorem on linear forms in
logarithms \cite{Matveev}: in fixed degree and for a fixed number of
logarithms, a nonzero form $\Lambda=\sum b_j\log\xi_j$ satisfies
$\log|\Lambda|\ge-C\prod_j H_j\log(eB)$, where
$H_j\ge\max\{dH(\xi_j),|\log\xi_j|,1\}$ and
$B\ge\max_j\{1,|b_j|\}$.
Apply it to
$(n+3)\operatorname{Log}\Gamma+\operatorname{Log}\omega_n
-2k\operatorname{Log}(-1)$, with imaginary part in $[-\pi,\pi]$.
For $n\ne2$ this form is nonzero by \eqref{partialfractions}; its
coefficients are $O(n)$ and its only varying height is $O(\log(n+2))$.
Since
$|C_n^3(h)|=(\sqrt2/7^{5/2})|Q_n(\alpha)|
|\Gamma^{n+3}\omega_n-1|$ and $|Q_n(\alpha)|\ge7(n+1)^2$,
the first estimate follows.
Finally, $\Gamma=e^{2ia_*}$ is not a root of unity, since its trace is
$-3/2$ and hence it is not an algebraic integer.
The same theorem applied to
$m\operatorname{Log}\Gamma-2k\operatorname{Log}(-1)$ gives the second
estimate.
\end{proof}

All radial functions will be even and invariant under rotations fixing the
first axis. Let $[u]_4$ denote the coefficient of $Z_4$ in this class.

\begin{lemma}\label{jets}
There is a formal solution with volume $V_0$, $[R]_4=\varepsilon$,
$R=1+\varepsilon Z_4+O(\varepsilon^2)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{firstjet}
 \rho=\rho_*+\rho_1\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad
 H(\theta)=h+\varepsilon\{h_1+bZ_4(\cos\theta)\}+O(\varepsilon^2),
\end{equation}
where
$\rho_1=-49\sqrt7/(1200\pi)$, $h_1=7h/50$, and $b=-2h/5$.
Its endpoint map has formal rotation angle $2a(\varepsilon)$, with
$a(\varepsilon)=a_*+(\sqrt7/50)\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
For every fixed integer $N$, its expression in chord coordinates can be
truncated to give an analytic family $z^{(0)}(a)$ on $I_t$ whose exact
cap-volume, cap-energy, and total-volume residuals are $O(t^{N+1})$
in \eqref{lipnorm}, on a fixed positive strip.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The derivative of cap volume with respect to height at the ball is $-A$,
where $A=4\pi\sigma^3/3>0$, so the height can be eliminated order by
order. Write $f=Z_4$ and $R=1+\varepsilon(f+w)$ with $[w]_4=0$.
Divide the nonconstant energy equation and the volume equation by
$\varepsilon$.
At $(\varepsilon,w,\rho)=(0,0,\rho_*)$, the linear system consists of
$T_h$ on the nonconstant modes other than degree four, the nonzero volume
row on constants, and the degree-four density column
$(V_0c_4/A)f$.
Lemma~\ref{arithmetic} makes this system invertible at each finite order.
Each coefficient is a polynomial in the axial variable: rotation
equivariance bounds the degree of an output by the sum of the input
degrees. Thus every coefficient requires only finitely many inversions.
The constant part of the energy then determines its scalar value.

Radial integration gives, with $u=n\cdot\omega$,
\begin{equation}\label{radialintegrals}
 V=\frac14\int_{uR>H}\left(R^4-\frac{H^4}{u^4}\right)d\omega,
 \qquad
 J=\int_{uR>H}\left(\frac{uR^5}{5}-\frac{HR^4}{4}
                         +\frac{H^5}{20u^4}\right)d\omega.
\end{equation}
The moving boundary is near $u=h>0$ and is transverse, so these formulas
justify all the finite Taylor expansions just used.
For $R=1+\varepsilon f+\varepsilon^2g+\cdots$, the quadratic nonconstant
energy is
\begin{equation}\label{quadratic}
 T_hg+\frac12(4T_h+hC_h)(f^2)
       -\frac{(C_hf)^2}{2A}+\rho_1\partial_\rho T_hf.
\end{equation}
Since $U_4^2=U_0+U_2+U_4+U_6+U_8$, its degree-four equation is
$\beta_c+\kappa_\rho\rho_1=0$, where
$\beta_c=-49\pi\sigma/6000$ and
$\kappa_\rho=V_0c_4/A=-\pi^2h/5$.
The first volume equation gives
$H_1=(c_4/A)f-V_0\rho_1/A$, proving \eqref{firstjet}.

The endpoints $B_\pm(\theta)$ satisfy
$R(B_\pm)\cos(B_\pm-\theta)=H(\theta)$, with base derivatives
$\mp\sigma$.
Their first variations have mean separation
$2\sigma^{-1}((h-b)/5-h_1)=\sqrt7/25$.
The endpoint map $B_+\circ B_-^{-1}$ commutes with translation by $\pi$
and is reversible under $x\mapsto-x$.
Its formal conjugacy to a rotation is obtained recursively by solving
the mean-zero equation for translation by $2a_*$; the divisors are
$e^{2ima_*}-1$, which are nonzero by Lemma~\ref{arithmetic}.
The mean determines the rotation angle, and zero mean normalizes the
conjugacy. Reversibility makes this conjugacy odd.
It follows that the meridian can be written formally with endpoints
$\gamma(x\pm a)$.
Since $a'(0)=\sqrt7/50\ne0$, formal scalar inversion expresses all
unknowns in $a-a_*$.

Fix $N$ and carry out these operations only to that order.
The resulting coefficients are analytic on a common strip, and their
polynomial truncations have the stated first-order terms.
The cap map in chord coordinates is analytic near the circle, as verified
below. Its residual therefore vanishes to order $N+1$ in $a-a_*$;
its derivative vanishes to order $N$.
On $I_t$ this gives the asserted weighted Lipschitz estimate.
\end{proof}

\section{The cap equations and their linearization}

Let $\gamma(x)=(X(x),Y(x))$ be a counterclockwise meridian near
$(\cos x,\sin x)$, with $X$ even, $Y$ odd, and
$\gamma(x+\pi)=-\gamma(x)$.
Revolve its upper half about the first axis.
For a fixed parameter $a$ write $\gamma_\pm=\gamma(x\pm a)$ and put
$L=|\gamma_+-\gamma_-|$,
$n=((\gamma_+-\gamma_-)_2,-(\gamma_+-\gamma_-)_1)/L$,
$e=(-n_2,n_1)$, and $d=n\cdot\gamma_+$.
Square roots are continued analytically from the circle.
The normal has an odd angular lift $n=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ with
$\theta(x+\pi)=\theta(x)+\pi$ and $\theta'>0$.
Set $r(u,x)=n(x)\cdot\gamma(u)-d(x)$.
The cap arc is $(x-a,x+a)$.
Integration over the transverse three-dimensional balls gives
\begin{equation}\label{chordintegrals}
\begin{aligned}
 V_K&=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\int_0^{2\pi}Y^3X'\,du,&
 V&=-\frac{\pi}{3n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}r^2(3n_2Y-r)X'\,du,\\
 J&=-\frac{\pi}{12n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}r^3(4n_2Y-r)X'\,du,&
 A&=-\frac{\pi}{n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}r(2n_2Y-r)X'\,du.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here $A=-\partial_dV$ is the area of the cutting section.
For $n_2>0$, the formulas follow by integrating
$\pi(Y^2-z^2)$ and $\pi n_2(z-z_0)(Y^2-z^2)$ from
$z_0=(d-n_1X)/n_2$ to $Y$.
The signed lower meridian subtracts the lower primitive when an entire
transverse ball lies in the cap. This also proves the formulas when the
arc crosses an axis pole; reflection gives $n_2<0$.

The apparent poles at $n_2=0$ are removable on the analytic scales.
Each numerator in \eqref{chordintegrals} is odd and antiperiodic in $x$.
At $x=0$, symmetry gives $n_1'=d'=0$ and $r_x=n_2'Y$.
The first derivatives of the three numerator integrands consequently
vanish; their endpoint terms vanish because $r=0$.
Thus the numerators vanish to order at least three at $0$ and $\pi$,
while $n_2/\sin x$ is invertible.
Division by $\sin x$ on the vanishing parity classes costs at most one
derivative, by
$\sin(kx)/\sin x=U_{k-1}(\cos x)$ and
$(\cos(2kx)-1)/\sin x=-2\sin(kx)U_{k-1}(\cos x)$.
After $u=x+v$, all the other operations are multiplication,
differentiation, translation, integration on $[-a,a]$, and inversion of
nonvanishing analytic functions.
This proves analyticity of the cap map, including for complex $a$ on a
smaller strip. Its first three joint differentials have bounds by fixed
powers of the strip loss. The cancellations hold for every symmetric
curve and therefore for their differentials as well.

For $z=(\gamma,\nu,c)$ define
\begin{equation}\label{F}
 F(z,a)=(F_V,F_E,F_0)=(V-\nu,\ J+\nu d-c,\ V_K-V_0).
\end{equation}
The first two components are even and $\pi$-periodic.
For a variation write $\delta\gamma=\psi N+w\gamma'$, where
$N=(Y',-X')/v$, $v=|\gamma'|$, $\psi$ is even and $\pi$-periodic,
and $w$ is odd and $\pi$-periodic.
Put $d_\theta=d'/\theta'$, $\tau_\pm=e\cdot\gamma_\pm-d_\theta$,
$P=\tau_+\tau_-<0$, $\xi=\delta\theta$, and
$\zeta=\delta d-d_\theta\xi$.
Differentiating the incidence equations gives
\begin{equation}\label{incidence}
\begin{aligned}
 \xi&=-\frac{n\cdot(\delta\gamma_+-\delta\gamma_-)}{L},&
 \zeta&=\frac{\tau_+n\cdot\delta\gamma_-
                  -\tau_-n\cdot\delta\gamma_+}{L},\\
 \zeta_w&=\frac{\theta'P}{L}(w_+-w_-),&
 \xi_w&=\theta'\frac{\tau_+w_+-\tau_-w_-}{L}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
With $p=2Yv\psi$, the fixed-plane shape derivatives are
$C\psi=(\pi/n_2)\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pr\,du$ and
$T\psi=(\pi/(2n_2))\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pr^2\,du$.
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{linearization}
 \delta F_V=C\psi-A\zeta-\delta\nu+\frac{F_V'}{\theta'}\xi,
 \qquad
 \delta F_E=T\psi+d\delta\nu-\delta c
                  +\frac{F_E'}{\theta'}\xi-F_V\zeta.
\end{equation}
Let $A_z$ be the operator obtained by dropping the terms containing
$F_V,F_V',F_E'$, and retaining the exact total-volume row.
Thus $D_zF=A_z+B_z[F]$, where $B_z[f]$ is linear in these residual
components and has only finite derivative losses.
The tangential volume equation has coefficient
$c_V=-A\theta'P/L>0$ multiplying $w_+-w_-$.
Its solvability condition is
\begin{equation}\label{meanrow}
 \delta\nu\int_0^{2\pi}c_V^{-1}\,dx
 =\int_0^{2\pi}(C\psi-A\zeta_\psi-f_V)c_V^{-1}\,dx.
\end{equation}

We next reduce the normal equation to a differential equation with fixed
translations. In the following calculation, primes mean differentiation
with respect to $\theta$, and $t_\pm(\theta)$ are the endpoint parameters.
Write $\kappa=d+d''$, $S=\tau_++\tau_-$, and
$K_jp=\int_{t_-}^{t_+}pr^j\,du$.
If $B_j=K_jp$, direct differentiation using $r_{\theta\theta}=-r-\kappa$
gives
\begin{equation}\label{moments}
\begin{aligned}
 B_0'&=p_+t_+'-p_-t_-',\\
 B_1''+B_1+\kappa B_0&=p_+\tau_+t_+'-p_-\tau_-t_-',\\
 B_2'''+4B_2'+6\kappa B_1'+2\kappa'B_1
 &=2(p_+\tau_+^2t_+'-p_-\tau_-^2t_-').
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{reductioncoefficients}
\begin{gathered}
 a_{\rm loc}=\kappa S/P,\qquad b_{\rm loc}=S/P,\qquad
 c_{\rm loc}=-3\kappa/P,\qquad
 e_{\rm loc}=c_{\rm loc}-b_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}b_{\rm loc},\\
 q=(S-\kappa')/P-e_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}e_{\rm loc},\qquad
 M=b_{\rm loc}\partial_\theta+e_{\rm loc},\qquad
 f_0=-\frac{B_2'''+4B_2'}{2P}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Eliminating the endpoint values in \eqref{moments} yields
$(\partial_\theta-a_{\rm loc})(B_0-MB_1)=qB_1+f_0$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{factorization}
\begin{gathered}
 \Delta=(q')^2+16q^2,\qquad
 H=q''-2a_{\rm loc}q'+16q,\qquad \varpi=Hq'/\Delta,\\
 \upsilon=16+\varpi'+a_{\rm loc}'-a_{\rm loc}\varpi-a_{\rm loc}^2
                     -16Hq/\Delta,\\
 \mathcal P=\partial_\theta^2+\varpi\partial_\theta+\upsilon,
 \qquad
 \mathcal Q=q\partial_\theta+q(\varpi+a_{\rm loc})-q'.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Coefficient comparison proves the exact identity
$(\partial_\theta-a_{\rm loc})\mathcal Q=q\mathcal P$.
The first-order data in \eqref{firstjet} give
\begin{equation}\label{firstgeometry}
\begin{aligned}
 S_1&=\frac{28h}{25}(\sin4\theta-2\sin2\theta),&
 P_1&=-\frac{77}{200}+\frac{14}{25}\cos2\theta-\frac7{50}\cos4\theta,\\
 \kappa_1&=\frac{3h}{50}+\frac{12h}{25}\cos2\theta
                         +\frac{12h}{5}\cos4\theta,&
 q&=\varepsilon\frac{192h}{5}\sin4\theta+O(\varepsilon^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For example, the linearization of \eqref{reductioncoefficients} is
$q_1=-(S_1+S_1''+2\kappa_1')/\sigma^2
-(3hP_1'+3h^2S_1)/\sigma^4$.
Hence $\Delta/\varepsilon^2=16(192h/5)^2+O(\varepsilon)$,
$H=O(\varepsilon^2)$, $\varpi=O(\varepsilon)$, and
$\upsilon=16+O(\varepsilon)$ on a fixed complex strip.
In particular, the construction never divides by $q$.

On odd antiperiodic functions, $\partial_\theta^2+16$ is invertible,
since $|16-k^2|\ge7$ for odd $k$.
Thus its perturbation $\mathcal P$ is invertible with two derivatives in
the domain norm.
The odd, periodic coefficient $a_{\rm loc}$ has mean zero, so
$\partial_\theta-a_{\rm loc}$ has a periodic integrating factor and an
invertible antiperiodic boundary condition.
Every solution therefore has the form
$B_1=\mathcal Pu$, $B_0=\mathcal Wu+z_0$, where
$\mathcal W=M\mathcal P+\mathcal Q$ and
$z_0=(\partial_\theta-a_{\rm loc})^{-1}f_0$.
The two endpoint reconstructions are
\begin{equation}\label{endpointoperators}
 A_\pm u+g_\pm,
 \qquad
 A_\pm=\frac{(\partial_\theta^2+1)\mathcal P
                    +(\kappa-\tau_\mp\partial_\theta)\mathcal W}{Lt_\pm'},
 \qquad
 g_\pm=\frac{\kappa z_0-\tau_\mp z_0'}{Lt_\pm'}.
\end{equation}
Denominators multiply on the left.
Agreement means that these expressions have the same value at the same
meridian point.
It reconstructs an odd antiperiodic $p$, and $\psi=p/(2Yv)$ is analytic
because $Y/\sin x$ is invertible.
Conversely, comparison of \eqref{moments} with the actual integrals gives
\begin{equation}\label{reconstruction}
 B_0=K_0p,\qquad B_1=K_1p+C\sin\theta,\qquad
 B_2=K_2p-2Cd\sin\theta.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the first difference is constant and odd, the second lies in
the odd antiperiodic kernel of $\partial_\theta^2+1$, and the last follows
from
$(\partial_\theta^3+4\partial_\theta)(d\sin\theta)
=\kappa'\sin\theta+3\kappa\cos\theta$.
The operator $\partial_\theta^3+4\partial_\theta$ has no antiperiodic
kernel.
Taking $B_2=(2\sin\theta/\pi)(f+c_1)$ is therefore equivalent to
$T\psi+d\nu_1=f+c_1$, with $\nu_1=-\pi C$.

Pull everything back to $x$, so that
$\partial_\theta=(\theta')^{-1}\partial_x$ and
$t_\pm'=(\theta')^{-1}$.
Endpoint agreement is now
$\mathcal Lu+GB_2=0$, with
$\mathcal L=T_{-a}A_+-T_aA_-$; the operator $G$ is defined by the same
difference of the $g_\pm$ in \eqref{endpointoperators}.
The auxiliary equations above are solved after pullback, as small
perturbations of constant elliptic operators in $x$.
All the formulas have finite differential order, and their only small
geometric denominator is $\Delta\asymp t^2$ when $\varepsilon\asymp t$.
Their estimates and difference estimates consequently lose only finitely
many derivatives and a fixed power of $t^{-1}$.

Two finite-dimensional conditions must be retained in this reduction.
If $H=p^+-p^-$ is the difference of the endpoint reconstructions, then
\begin{equation}\label{momentidentity}
 \int XH\,du
 =\int\{-\sin\theta(B_1''+B_1+\kappa B_0)
              +(d\cos\theta-d'\sin\theta)B_0'\}\,d\theta=0.
\end{equation}
Integration by parts proves the last equality, using
$(d\cos\theta-d'\sin\theta)'=-\kappa\sin\theta$.
The identity holds for both terms of the compatibility equation
separately. Adding a column $\lambda X$ therefore forces $\lambda=0$.
The analogous $Y$ moment vanishes by parity.
Off compatibility, put $p^o=(p^++p^-)/2$, $\psi^o=p^o/(2Yv)$, and
$C^o=\int\sin\theta(B_1-K_1p^o)\,d\theta/\int\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$.
To invert the normal equation at prescribed density, modulo its critical
mode, use
$B_2=(2\sin\theta/\pi)(f+c_1+\eta Z_4(\cos x))$ and impose
$\delta V_K(\psi^o)=0$, $\lambda_4(\psi^o)=0$, $C^o=0$, where
\begin{equation}\label{projections}
 \lambda_4(v)=\frac5\pi\int_0^\pi v(x)(\cos4x-\cos6x)\,dx,
 \qquad
 \lambda_0(v)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi v(x)(1-\cos2x)\,dx.
\end{equation}

We record the reference finite system explicitly.
At the sphere, input $u_k\sin(kx)$ has compatibility and reconstruction
multipliers
\begin{equation}\label{referenceendpoint}
\begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_k&=\frac{16-k^2}{\sigma}
       \left\{(k^2-10/7)\sin(ka_*)+\frac{3k}{\sqrt7}\cos(ka_*)\right\},\\
 R_k&=\frac{16-k^2}{2\sigma}
       \left\{(10/7-k^2)\cos(ka_*)+\frac{3k}{\sqrt7}\sin(ka_*)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
A source $b_k\sin(kx)$ has compatibility coefficient
$(4-k^2)[k\cos(ka_*)-(h/\sigma)\sin(ka_*)]b_k/(2\sigma^2)$.
Thus $R_1=180/(7\sqrt7)$, $R_5=2160/(7\sqrt7)$, and the $\eta$ column
has coefficient $-336h/(5\pi)$ at mode five.
The $X$ column removes output mode one and the amplitude row removes
input mode five.
For the remaining constant block, writing $s_1=3/(4\sigma^3)$ gives
$p^o=(R_1u_1+2s_1c_1/\pi)\sin x$ and
$C^o=15u_1-(a_*-h\sigma)(R_1u_1+2s_1c_1/\pi)$.
The volume and amplitude rows are $\pi^2p_1$ and $(5/2)p_5$.
The determinant of the rows $p_1,C^o$ is
$-45/(2\pi\sigma^3)\ne0$.
This proves invertibility of the complete finite augmentation.

These rows and columns have analytic Fourier tails of size $O(t)$ away
from their finite reference support, on fixed inner strips.
For the volume row use $\delta V_K=\pi\int Yp^o$.
For the amplitude row, the weight in $p^o$ is a multiple of $\sin5x$
at the sphere and its apparent pole remains removable.
For $C^o$, changing the order in
$\int w(x)\int_{-a}^a p^o(x+v)r(x+v,x)\,dv\,dx$
gives the analytic adjoint weight
$\int_{-a}^a w(u-v)r(u,u-v)\,dv$.
Differentiation and fixed translations preserve these tails.
The mean row \eqref{meanrow} has a generally nonzero complementary part
and will be treated separately.

\section{Inverting the complementary equation}

Choose $\tau>\tau_*+1$ and a sufficiently small fixed $\gamma_0>0$.
We first restrict the parameter to
\begin{equation}\label{homogeneous}
 \mathcal H_t=\{a\in I_t:|2\sin(ma)|\ge
             \gamma_0(1+|m|)^{-\tau}\text{ for every nonzero even }m\}.
\end{equation}
In the $x$ coordinate, the leading coefficients of $A_\pm$ are
$\alpha_\pm=-\tau_\mp/(\tau_\pm L(\theta')^3)$.
Changing the sign of the compatibility operator gives
$\widetilde{\mathcal L}=B_+T_a-B_-T_{-a}$, with positive leading
coefficients $\beta_+=\alpha_-(x+a)$ and
$\beta_-=\alpha_+(x-a)$.
They satisfy $\beta_+(-x)=\beta_-(x)$.
Solve
$b(x+a)-b(x-a)=\log\beta_- -\log\beta_+$ with zero mean, and set
$w=e^b$, $e_0=\beta_+w(x+a)=\beta_-w(x-a)$.
The solution $b$ is real and even.
On odd Fourier indices let $D=-i\partial_x$.
The product rule gives the exact finite identity
\begin{equation}\label{balanced}
 e_0^{-1}\widetilde{\mathcal L}M_wD^{-4}
 =P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a},\qquad
 P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^4p_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j},
\end{equation}
where $M_w$ denotes multiplication by $w$.
For example, if $B_\pm=\sum_{j=0}^4b_{\pm,j}D^j$, the coefficient of
$D^{-l}$ on the left is
$e_0^{-1}\sum_{j=4-l}^4\binom{j}{4-l}b_{\pm,j}D^{j-4+l}w(x\pm a)$.
The coefficient for $l=0$ is one.
The lower coefficients satisfy
$\overline{p_{\pm,j}}=(-1)^jp_{\pm,j}$ and
$p_{-,j}(x)=(-1)^jp_{+,j}(-x)$.
Solving the equation for $b$ costs a fixed power of a strip loss.
The same holds for its parameter difference quotients, by the identity
$d(a)^{-1}-d(b)^{-1}=(d(b)-d(a))/(d(a)d(b))$.
This requires lower bounds only at the two parameters in question.

For a Fourier matrix set
$\norm B_{\B_r}=\sup_k\sum_j e^{r|j-k|}|B_{jk}|$.
This is an algebra norm and controls $\A_s\to\A_s$ for $0\le s\le r$.
Write $\ell_k=\log(2+|k|)$ and
$\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}
=\sup_ke^{c\ell_k^4}\sum_je^{r|j-k|}|\mathcal R_{jk}|$.
Then
$\norm{B\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}
\le\norm B_{\B_r}\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}$.
A symbol $b(x,k)$ denotes the operator
$u\mapsto\sum_kb(x,k)u_ke^{ikx}$; its $\B_r$ norm is
$\sup_k\norm{b(\cdot,k)}_r$.

\begin{lemma}\label{normalform}
Let $\mathcal L=P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a}$, where
$P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^Jp_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j}$ have the symmetries in
\eqref{balanced} and bounded analytic coefficients, and assume
\eqref{homogeneous}.
Fix constant reference coefficients $p^0_{\pm,j}$ with these symmetries,
write $P_\pm^0(k)=1+\sum_{j=1}^Jp_{\pm,j}^0k^{-j}$, and put
$\eta=\max_{\pm,j}\norm{p_{\pm,j}-p^0_{\pm,j}}_r$.
There are operators $Q,E$, constant symbols $M_\pm(k)$, and a remainder
$\mathcal R$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{normalidentity}
 \mathcal LQ=E\mathcal D+\mathcal R,
 \qquad \mathcal D=M_+(D)T_a-M_-(D)T_{-a}.
\end{equation}
For fixed positive $c,C,C_*$ and $r'=r-C_*\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{normalestimates}
 \norm{Q-I}_{\B_{r'}}+\norm{E-I}_{\B_{r'}}
 +\sup_k|k|\sum_\pm|M_\pm(k)-P_\pm^0(k)|
 +\norm{\mathcal R}_{r',c}^{\sharp}
 \le\eta e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)}.
\end{equation}
For differences of two inputs at the same parameter, replace $\eta$ by
their coefficient distance. The estimate also holds in Lipschitz norms on
every closed subset of $\mathcal H_t$, with $\eta$ replaced by the
corresponding input norm and fixed enlarged constants.
The construction is independent of the strip on which it is estimated.
If $E^{-1}$ is bounded, then, across another strip loss,
\begin{equation}\label{twosided}
 |(E^{-1}\mathcal R)_{jk}|
 \le C\eta e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)}
 e^{-(r-C_*\delta)|j-k|-c_1(\ell_j^4+\ell_k^4)}
\end{equation}
for a fixed $c_1>0$.
Moreover, $M_- =\overline{M_+}$.
If $|M_+(k)|$ is bounded away from zero, the diagonal is
$d_k=2iA_k\sin(ka+\phi_k)$, with $A_k>0$.
On a fixed strip, bounded unweighted Lipschitz norms of the input
coefficients give $\Lip\phi_k\le C/|k|$ for perturbations of the reference
symbols used below.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Seek formal symbols
$Q=1+\sum_{n\ge1}q_nk^{-n}$,
$E=1+\sum_{n\ge1}e_nk^{-n}$, and
$M_\pm=1+\sum_{n\ge1}m_{\pm,n}k^{-n}$, with $q_n,e_n$ of mean zero,
satisfying $P_\pm\#Q_{\pm a}=EM_\pm$.
The formal product is
$p\#q=\sum_{\alpha\ge0}(\partial_k^\alpha p)D_x^\alpha q/\alpha!$.
With $p_{\pm,n}=0$ for $n>J$, its known order-$n$ coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{symbolrecursion}
 f_{\pm,n}=p_{\pm,n}
 +\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le J,\ l\ge1,\ \alpha\ge0\\j+l+\alpha=n}}
 (-1)^\alpha\binom{j+\alpha-1}{\alpha}
 p_{\pm,j}D_x^\alpha q_l(x\pm a)
 -\sum_{b=1}^{n-1}e_bm_{\pm,n-b}.
\end{equation}
The unique normalized recursion is
$m_{\pm,n}=\av{f_{\pm,n}}$,
$q_n(x+a)-q_n(x-a)=-\Pi_0(f_{+,n}-f_{-,n})$, and
$e_n=q_n(x+a)+f_{+,n}-m_{+,n}$, where $\Pi_0$ removes the mean.
Only the homogeneous divisors in \eqref{homogeneous} occur.

An expression of grade $n$ has at most $n$ coefficient factors,
$2n-1$ normalization operations, and total derivative order at most $n$.
Allocate $\delta/(6n)$ to each operation along a branch of its expression
tree. A derivative of order $\alpha$ costs
$\alpha!(6n/\delta)^\alpha$, and a homogeneous inverse costs
$C\gamma_0^{-1}(6n/\delta)^\tau$.
Counting the distributions of grades and increasing fixed constants gives
\begin{equation}\label{symbolbound}
 \norm{q_n}_{r-\delta}+\norm{e_n}_{r-\delta}
 +\sum_\pm|m_{\pm,n}-p^0_{\pm,n}|
 \le \eta(C\delta^{-B})^n(n!)^\kappa.
\end{equation}
Subtracting two such expressions marks one factor and proves the
difference estimate. For parameter differences, use the reciprocal
difference identity at the marked homogeneous inverse and
$\norm{T_au-T_bu}_{r-\delta}\le |a-b|\delta^{-1}\norm u_r$.
Larger fixed $B,\kappa$ give the same bound in \eqref{lipnorm}.
For constant reference coefficients the normalized solution has
$q_n=e_n=0$, $m_{\pm,n}=p^0_{\pm,n}$, which explains the factor $\eta$.

For every odd $k$ fix $N(k)=\lfloor\ell_k^3\rfloor$.
Define $Q,E$ by their sums through $N(k)$ and set
$M_\pm(k)=P_\pm^0(k)+\sum_{n\le N(k)}(m_{\pm,n}-p^0_{\pm,n})k^{-n}$.
The reference polynomial is retained exactly.
For $A\ge1$ the elementary estimates
\begin{equation}\label{truncationbound}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{n=1}^{N(k)}A^n(n!)^\kappa|k|^{-n}
 &\le |k|^{-1}e^{C(1+\log A)^4},\\
 A^{N(k)+1}((N(k)+1)!)^\kappa|k|^{-N(k)-1}
 &\le e^{C(1+\log A)^4-c\ell_k^4}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
follow by separating $\ell_k\ge C_\kappa(1+\log A)$, where the ratios
are at most $1/2$, from the remaining range, where
$N(k)=O((1+\log A)^3)$.
They prove the bounds for $Q,E,M_\pm$.

To verify the remainder estimate for the actual operators, an exact
Fourier product contains $(k+\nu)^{-j}(q_l)_\nu k^{-l}$.
The index $k+\nu$ is odd and never zero.
For $|\nu|<|k|/2$, Taylor expansion of the reciprocal through total grade
$N(k)$ has remainder bounded by
$C^{s+j}|k|^{-j-l-s}\delta^{-s}s!\norm{q_l}_{r-\delta}$,
where $j+l+s=N(k)+1$.
Terms already above that grade use
$|(k+\nu)^{-j}|\le2^J|k|^{-j}$.
For $|\nu|\ge|k|/2$, use the exact bound
$|(k+\nu)^{-j}|\le1$ and, across a further margin,
$e^{-\delta|\nu|}|\nu|^\alpha
\le e^{-\delta|k|/4}\alpha!(2/\delta)^\alpha$.
Equations \eqref{symbolbound}--\eqref{truncationbound} bound all these
tails by $\eta e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)-c\ell_k^4}$.
The terms of $EM_\pm$ above grade $N(k)$ obey the same estimate.
The formal cancellations therefore give the exact identity
\eqref{normalidentity} and the last bound in \eqref{normalestimates}.
Subtraction proves the identical bounds for increments and parameter
difference quotients.

The raw bound gives exponential decay in $|j-k|$ and
$e^{-c\ell_k^4}$ in the input index.
The inequality
$\ell_j^4\le C(\ell_k^4+\log^4(2+|j-k|))$, followed by absorption of
$\log^4(2+|j-k|)$ into a small multiple of $|j-k|$, gives
\eqref{twosided}. Left multiplication by $E^{-1}$ preserves the raw
bound by the matrix product inequality above.
The recursion also gives
$\overline{q_n}=(-1)^nq_n$, $q_n(-x)=(-1)^nq_n(x)$, and the same
identities for $e_n$, together with
$m_{-,n}=(-1)^nm_{+,n}=\overline{m_{+,n}}$.
The even cutoff $N(k)$ preserves these symmetries.
Finally \eqref{symbolbound}--\eqref{truncationbound}, on a fixed strip,
bound the parameter difference quotient of $M_+$ by $C/|k|$.
Taking its argument near a nonzero reference symbol proves the phase
estimate.
\end{proof}

At the sphere the reference symbols in \eqref{balanced} are
\begin{equation}\label{referencesymbol}
 M_+^0(k)=\frac{(k^2-16)(k^2-10/7+(3i/\sqrt7)k)}{k^4},
 \qquad
 d_k^*=-16i\sigma^3\frac{k^2-16}{k^4}C_{k-3}^3(h)
 \quad(k\ge3\text{ odd}).
\end{equation}
The second identity follows by differentiating
$U_{k-1}(\cos a)=\sin(ka)/\sin a$ twice.
Direct substitution gives $d_1^*=0$.
Lemma~\ref{arithmetic} shows that the only other exceptional positive
index is five, and that
$|d_k^*|\ge ce^{-C\ell_k^2}$ off $|k|=1,5$.
The moduli of $M_+^0(k)$ are bounded below: for $k\ge5$ use
$(1-16/k^2)(1-10/(7k^2))\ge297/875$, and the values at $1,3$ are
$90\sqrt2/7$ and $\sqrt{3376}/81$.
Thus sufficiently small perturbations have
$0<A_-\le A_k\le A_+$ and phases with the Lipschitz bound in
Lemma~\ref{normalform}.

Let $\mathcal F=\{-5,-1,1,5\}$ and
$\mathcal H=(2\Z+1)\setminus\mathcal F$.
Impose, for a fixed $\gamma>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{diagonalcondition}
 |d_k|\ge\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}\qquad(k\in\mathcal H).
\end{equation}
If the normalized remainder in \eqref{twosided} has size $O(t)$, then
$\norm{\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}
(E^{-1}\mathcal R)_{\mathcal H\mathcal H}}_{\B_s}\le Ct$.
Indeed, the factors $e^{\ell_j^3-c_1\ell_j^4}$ are summable.
The Neumann series therefore gives a complementary inverse whose cost
across a margin $\delta$ is at most $Ce^{C\log^3(e/\delta)}$.
The same argument in Lipschitz norms uses the reciprocal difference
identity; the extra factor $e^{\ell_j^3}$ is still
absorbed by $e^{-c_1\ell_j^4}$.

The finite augmentation at the end of the preceding section is eliminated
before applying this inverse.
Its finite block is uniformly invertible, while its rows and columns
outside $\mathcal F$ are $O(t)$ and decay exponentially in their
respective Fourier indices.
Its Schur correction is consequently a finite-rank matrix of size
$O(t^2)$ with exponential decay in both indices.
It has the same bound as \eqref{twosided}, after a fixed loss, and gives
the inverse of the physical normal equation at prescribed density,
modulo its amplitude mode.
Across fixed positive gaps this inverse is uniformly bounded as
$t\downarrow0$.

It remains to solve for the amplitude and density.
Use a fixed chain of positive strips below the eventual limiting width
for the following scalar pairings.
The cap integrals give $T_\varepsilon-T_h=O(\varepsilon)$ across these
gaps. Since $T_hZ_4=0$ and $\lambda_4T_h=0$, both the amplitude column
into the complement and its critical output row are $O(\varepsilon)$.
The nonconstant density column is
$V_0(d-\lambda_0d)=\varepsilon\kappa_\rho f+O(\varepsilon^2)$,
so its complementary part is $O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Correcting the volume gauge changes these orders only at second order,
because $T_h1$ is constant.
The critical quadratic equation is
$\beta_c\tau^2+\kappa_\rho\tau(\rho-\rho_*)+
O((|\tau|+|\rho-\rho_*|)^3)=0$.
At \eqref{firstjet} its amplitude derivative is
$\varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
A first-order change to chord coordinates adds $T_hv$ to the input
correction and acts on $T_hf=0$ in the output, so this critical
coefficient is unchanged.
The mean condition \eqref{meanrow}, normalized to density coefficient
one, has amplitude coefficient $-2\rho_1$ at the sphere, since
$\av{f}_x=1/5$ and $(c_4-Ah)/(5V_0)=2\rho_1$.
The remaining scalar matrix is therefore
\begin{equation}\label{scalarmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)&
       \varepsilon\kappa_\rho+O(\varepsilon^2)\\
 -2\rho_1+O(\varepsilon)&1+O(\varepsilon)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Its complementary columns have orders $O(\varepsilon),O(\varepsilon^2)$
and its rows have orders $O(\varepsilon),O(1)$.
The Schur correction thus has top row
$O(\varepsilon^2),O(\varepsilon^3)$ and bottom row
$O(\varepsilon),O(\varepsilon^2)$.
The determinant is
$\varepsilon(\beta_c+2\kappa_\rho\rho_1)+O(\varepsilon^2)
=-\varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)$, bounded below by $c t$.
Solving this system makes \eqref{meanrow} hold, and
\eqref{homogeneous} then gives the odd tangential variation $w$.
For a nonzero total-volume forcing, first subtract the variation given
by a constant normal displacement with that volume derivative.
Its coefficient is uniformly well defined near the sphere.

We have proved that, whenever the normalizers and their inverses are
bounded and the smoothing remainder has size $O(t)$, $A_z$ has a right
inverse $N_z$ on every parity-compatible residual triple, with
\begin{equation}\label{inverseestimate}
 \norm{N_zf}^{\Lip}_{r-C\delta,t;G}
 \le t^{-P}e^{C\log^P(e/\delta)}
          \norm f^{\Lip}_{r,t;G}.
\end{equation}
Here $P,C$ are fixed, $G$ is any closed set satisfying
\eqref{homogeneous} and \eqref{diagonalcondition}, and the curve has the
controlled first-order expansion \eqref{firstjet}.
All finite geometric differentiations and the scalar inverse are
included in $P$.
Only the scalar pairings use the fixed inner gaps; reconstruction uses
the current margin $\delta$.

\section{Convergence}

Fix the constants in the arithmetic and homogeneous estimates, positive
initial and limiting widths $r_0>r_\infty>0$, and the inner strips for
the scalar pairings.
Fix $\gamma>0$ so small that
$|d_k^*|\ge4\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $k\in\mathcal H$.
This is possible by \eqref{referencesymbol}.
All the constants and the finite derivative orders in
\eqref{inverseestimate} are now fixed.
We shall choose a sufficiently large, fixed truncation order in
Lemma~\ref{jets}, and only then decrease $t$.

We first explain how the operator estimates persist as widths decrease.
Choose $\delta_j=c_r(j+1)^{-2}$ and a fixed integer $L$ large enough for
the finitely many margins used in one step, so that
$r_{j+1}=r_j-L\delta_j$ and $\sum_jL\delta_j<r_0-r_\infty$.
At width $r_j$, retain the curve and the finitely many derivatives needed
for the geometric coefficients, the balancing function, $Q_j,E_j$ and
their inverses, the raw remainder in \eqref{normalestimates}, its
two-index bound, and the finite augmentation.
Initially these are constructed across fixed margins from the seed on a
larger strip, and their differences from the reference are $O(t)$.
At the next step, allocate successive margins to reconstruction, the
geometric and balancing increments, and
Lemma~\ref{normalform} applied to the resulting coefficient increments.
If $E_{j+1}-E_j$ is small, a Neumann series gives $E_{j+1}^{-1}$ on an
intermediate strip. Use the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{actualincrement}
 E_{j+1}^{-1}\mathcal R_{j+1}-E_j^{-1}\mathcal R_j
 =E_{j+1}^{-1}(\mathcal R_{j+1}-\mathcal R_j)
 +(E_{j+1}^{-1}-E_j^{-1})\mathcal R_j.
\end{equation}
Both terms retain the same raw smoothing exponent.
Convert this increment to \eqref{twosided} across one further margin,
keeping the raw remainder separately for the next step.
For the finite augmentation, use
$\Delta(UV)=(\Delta U)V+U_{j+1}\Delta V$ and the corresponding inverse
identity.
Its analytic row and column tails have the required smoothing bound
because
$\sup_ke^{-\delta|k|+c\ell_k^4}\le e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)}$.
Thus every update costs at most
$t^{-P}e^{C\log^P(e/\delta_j)}$ times the actual correction.
The exponent in the smoothing bound stays fixed.
The scalar matrix \eqref{scalarmatrix} is solved afterward and does not
enter these updates.

Let $z_0$ be the seed and restrict it first to $\mathcal H_t$.
Set $\Gamma_j=\gamma(1+2^{-j})$ and
$G_0=\{a\in\mathcal H_t:|d_{0,k}(a)|\ge
\Gamma_0e^{-\ell_k^3}\text{ for every }k\in\mathcal H\}$.
Inductively, on $G_j$ define
\begin{equation}\label{newton}
 f_j=F(z_j,a),\qquad v_j=-N_{z_j}f_j,\qquad z_{j+1}=z_j+v_j,
\end{equation}
construct its new diagonal, and let
$G_{j+1}=\{a\in G_j:|d_{j+1,k}(a)|\ge
\Gamma_{j+1}e^{-\ell_k^3}\text{ for every }k\in\mathcal H\}$.
All these sets are closed.
Every inverse and every difference quotient is taken on the current
set, and restriction to the next set can only decrease the norms.

Since $A_{z_j}N_{z_j}=I$ and $D_zF=A_z+B_z[F]$, the actual residual on
$G_j$ satisfies
$F(z_j+v_j)=B_{z_j}[f_j]v_j+
F(z_j+v_j)-F(z_j)-D_zF(z_j)v_j$.
The first term is bilinear; the Taylor remainder is quadratic.
The cap-map estimates established after \eqref{chordintegrals}, including
its third joint differential for the parameter difference quotient, give
\begin{equation}\label{quadraticiteration}
 E_{j+1}\le t^{-P}e^{C\log^P(e/\delta_j)}E_j^2,
 \qquad

\begin{abstract}
We construct nonspherical, centrally symmetric, strictly convex bodies of
revolution in four dimensions with real-analytic boundary that float in
equilibrium in every orientation.
Their relative densities tend to an explicit value near $0.218294$ as the
bodies approach the unit ball.
The construction corrects a finite-order deformation by an analytic Newton
iteration on sets of chord parameters of asymptotically full relative measure.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A homogeneous convex body of relative density $\rho$ floats in equilibrium
in a direction $n$ when the cap of volume $\rho\vol K$ cut off normal to $n$
has its centroid on the line through the centroid of $K$ parallel to $n$.
Ryabogin constructed nonspherical examples floating in every orientation
at density $1/2$ \cite{Ryabogin22}; central symmetry at that density forces
a convex body to be a ball \cite{Florentin}.
Wegner's formal constructions concern other densities \cite{Wegner}.
Here we obtain exact centrally symmetric analytic examples in $\R^4$.

Put $Z_l=U_l/(l+1)$, where $U_l(\cos x)=\sin((l+1)x)/\sin x$, and set
\begin{equation}\label{constants}
 h=\frac1{\sqrt8},\quad \sigma=\sqrt{\frac78},\quad
 a_*=\arccos h,\quad V_0=\frac{\pi^2}{2},\quad
 \rho_*=\frac{a_*}{\pi}-\frac{19\sqrt7}{96\pi}.
\end{equation}
Thus $Z_l$ is the normalized zonal harmonic on $S^3$ and
$\rho_*V_0=(4\pi/3)\int_h^1(1-s^2)^{3/2}\,ds$.

\begin{theorem}\label{main}
Fix $0<c_1<c_2$. For all sufficiently small $t>0$ there is a closed set
$G_t\subset I_t=[a_*+c_1t,a_*+c_2t]$, with $|G_t|/|I_t|\to1$, such that
each $a\in G_t$ gives a centrally symmetric, strictly convex body of
revolution $K_a\subset\R^4$ of volume $V_0$, with real-analytic boundary,
floating in equilibrium in every orientation. Its radial function and
relative density satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{asymptotics}
 R_a=1+\varepsilon Z_4+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad
 \rho_a=\rho_*-\frac{49\sqrt7}{1200\pi}\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad
 a-a_*=\frac{\sqrt7}{50}\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2).
\end{equation}
Here $\varepsilon>0$ is the degree-four radial coefficient, the remainders
are uniform on a fixed complex angular strip, and $a$ is half the
separation of the endpoint parameters in an analytic parametrization of
the meridian. In particular, nonspherical examples occur arbitrarily
close to the ball at densities different from $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

For a centrally symmetric body write
$V(n,d)=\vol(K\cap\{n\cdot z>d\})$ and
$J(n,d)=\int_K(n\cdot z-d)_+\,dz$.
At fixed cap volume $\nu$, choose $d(n)$ by $V(n,d(n))=\nu$.
Since $J_d=-V$, the energy $\mathcal E(n)=J(n,d(n))+\nu d(n)$ satisfies
$D\mathcal E(n)[e]=\int_{n\cdot z>d(n)}e\cdot z\,dz$ for $e\perp n$.
Thus equilibrium in every orientation is equivalent to constant $\mathcal E$;
see also \cite{Ryabogin23}.

All estimates allow a strip loss $\delta>0$ and use the usual product
and Cauchy inequalities. Constants are independent of $t$, Fourier

\section{Expansion at the ball}

Let $C_h,T_h$ be the spherical integral operators with kernels
$\mathbf1_{\{n\cdot\omega>h\}}$ and $(n\cdot\omega-h)_+$, using surface
measure on $S^3$. The Gegenbauer convention is
$(1-2xz+z^2)^{-\lambda}=\sum_{l\ge0}C_l^{(\lambda)}(x)z^l$.

\begin{lemma}\label{arithmetic}
For $l\ge2$ the multipliers of $C_h,T_h$ are
\begin{equation}\label{multipliers}
 c_l(h)=\frac{8\pi(1-h^2)^{3/2}C_{l-1}^{(2)}(h)}{l(l+1)(l+2)},\qquad
 t_l(h)=\frac{32\pi(1-h^2)^{5/2}C_{l-2}^{(3)}(h)}
 {(l-1)l(l+1)(l+2)(l+3)}.
\end{equation}
At the height \eqref{constants}, $C_n^{(3)}(h)=0$ exactly for $n=2$,
and for some $c,C,\tau_*>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{arithmeticbounds}
 |C_n^{(3)}(h)|\ge c(n+1)^2e^{-C\log^2(n+2)}\quad(n\ne2),\qquad
 |2\sin(ma_*)|\ge c(1+|m|)^{-\tau_*}\quad(m\ne0).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Funk--Hecke and the Gegenbauer identities \cite[Chapter 18]{DLMF} give
\eqref{multipliers}. Put $\alpha=(1+i\sqrt7)/2$, $\beta=\bar\alpha$,
and $Q_n(X)=-(7n^2+45n+62)+(6n+18)X$. Partial fractions give
\begin{equation}\label{partialfractions}
 (\sqrt2)^nC_n^{(3)}(h)
 =\frac{\alpha^{n+3}Q_n(\beta)-\beta^{n+3}Q_n(\alpha)}{2(i\sqrt7)^5}.
\end{equation}
The coprime ideals $(\alpha),(\beta)$ have norm two, so a zero forces
$2^{n+3}\mid M(n)$, where
$M(n)=49n^4+588n^3+2569n^2+4830n+3376$.
This fails for $n\ge21$, since $M(21)<2^{24}$ and
$M(n+1)/M(n)\le((n+1)/n)^4<2$ for $n\ge6$; the finite check leaves
only $n=0,2$, and $C_0^{(3)}=1$.

For the bounds, set $\Gamma=\alpha/\beta=e^{2ia_*}$ and
$\omega_n=Q_n(\beta)/Q_n(\alpha)$.
Their degrees are fixed and the logarithmic height of $\omega_n$ is
$O(\log(n+2))$. Matveev's theorem \cite{Matveev}, applied to
$(n+3)\Log\Gamma+\Log\omega_n-2j\Log(-1)$ with imaginary part in
$[-\pi,\pi]$, gives $|\Gamma^{n+3}\omega_n-1|\ge e^{-C\log^2(n+2)}$
for $n\ne2$.
Use \eqref{partialfractions} and $|Q_n(\alpha)|\ge7(n+1)^2$.
The same theorem with fixed heights gives the sine bound, since
$\Gamma$ has nonintegral trace $-3/2$ and is not a root of unity.
\end{proof}

Write $f(x)=Z_4(\cos x)$ and let
$\lambda_l(v)=(l+1)\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi
v(x)(\cos(lx)-\cos((l+2)x))\,dx$ extract its zonal coefficients.

\begin{proposition}\label{seed}
For each fixed $N$ the cap equations \eqref{F} have an analytic
approximation $z^{[N]}(a)$ with residual $O(t^N)$ in $\norm\cdot^{\Lip}$
on a fixed strip. Its first-order data are
\begin{equation}\label{branch}
 R=1+\varepsilon f+O(\varepsilon^2),\quad
 \rho=\rho_*+\rho_1\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2),\quad
 H=h+\varepsilon(h_1+bf)+O(\varepsilon^2),
\end{equation}
where $\rho_1=-49\sqrt7/(1200\pi)$, $h_1=7h/50$, $b=-2h/5$, and
$a-a_*=(\sqrt7/50)\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The height is eliminated by $V_H=-A_*\ne0$, where
$A_*=4\pi\sigma^3/3$. Write $R=1+\varepsilon(f+w)$, $\lambda_4(w)=0$,
and divide the nonconstant energy and volume equations by $\varepsilon$.
At the ball their linearization is $T_h$ on the noncritical modes,
the volume row on constants, and the critical density column
$(V_0c_4/A_*)f$, where $c_4=-7\pi h\sigma/15\ne0$.
Lemma~\ref{arithmetic} therefore determines each finite jet; rotation
equivariance bounds the harmonic degree at order $j$ by $4j$.
For $R=1+\varepsilon f+\varepsilon^2g$, the quadratic nonconstant energy is
$T_hg+\tfrac12(4T_h+hC_h)(f^2)-(C_hf)^2/(2A_*)+
\rho_1V_0C_hf/A_*$.
Since $\lambda_4(f^2)=1/5$, its critical equation is
$\beta_c+\kappa_\rho\rho_1=0$, with
\begin{equation}\label{critical}
 \beta_c=\frac{hc_4-c_4^2/A_*}{10}=-\frac{49\pi\sigma}{6000},\qquad
 \kappa_\rho=\frac{V_0c_4}{A_*}=-\frac{\pi^2h}{5}.
\end{equation}
The volume equation gives $H_1=(c_4f-V_0\rho_1)/A_*$.

The endpoint map of the prescribed-volume chords is reversible under
reflection and commutes with translation by $\pi$.
Its normalized formal conjugacy to translation by $2a(\varepsilon)$ is
obtained from $u(x+2a_*)-u(x)=g-\av g$; the mean fixes $a$, and
reversibility makes the conjugacy odd.
Differentiating the endpoint equation
$R(B_\pm)\cos(B_\pm-\theta)=H(\theta)$ gives
$a'(0)=\sigma^{-1}((h-b)/5-h_1)=\sqrt7/50$.
Invert this scalar series and truncate in $a-a_*$. The coefficients
are trigonometric polynomials, so the strip is independent of $N$;
analyticity of the cap map and Taylor's theorem give the residual estimate.
\end{proof}

\section{The linearized equations}

Let $\gamma=(X,Y)$ be a meridian near $(\cos x,\sin x)$, with $X$ even,
$Y$ odd, and $\gamma(x+\pi)=-\gamma(x)$. Write
$\gamma_\pm=\gamma(x\pm a)$, $L=|\gamma_+-\gamma_-|$,
$n=((\gamma_+-\gamma_-)_2,-(\gamma_+-\gamma_-)_1)/L$,
$e=(-n_2,n_1)$, $d=n\cdot\gamma_+$, and
$v(u,x)=n(x)\cdot\gamma(u)-d(x)$.
The normal angle $\theta$ is odd, $n=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$,
and $\theta'>0$. Transverse integration gives
\begin{equation}\label{caps}
\begin{aligned}
 V_K&=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\int_0^{2\pi}Y^3X'\,du,&
 V&=-\frac{\pi}{3n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}v^2(3n_2Y-v)X'\,du,\\
 J&=-\frac{\pi}{12n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}v^3(4n_2Y-v)X'\,du,&
 A&=-\frac{\pi}{n_2^3}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}v(2n_2Y-v)X'\,du.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here $A=-V_d$. The numerators are odd antiperiodic functions with
third-order zeros at the poles: their first derivatives vanish by
$v=0$ at the endpoints and $v_x=n_2'Y$ at a pole.
Since $n_2/\sin x$ is invertible and division by $\sin x$ on the
vanishing parity classes costs one derivative, these formulas define
analytic maps with fixed finite losses, also for their joint differentials.
The equations to solve are
\begin{equation}\label{F}
 F(z,a)=(V-\nu,J+\nu d-c,V_K-V_0)=0,\qquad z=(\gamma,\nu,c).
\end{equation}

For a variation write $\delta\gamma=\psi N+w\gamma'$, where
$s=|\gamma'|$, $N=(Y',-X')/s$, $\psi$ is even and $\pi$-periodic,
and $w$ is odd and $\pi$-periodic. Set
$p=2Ys\psi$, $\tau_\pm=e\cdot\gamma_\pm-d_\theta$,
$P=\tau_+\tau_-<0$, $\xi=\delta\theta$, and
$\zeta=\delta d-d_\theta\xi$.
Endpoint incidence and shape differentiation give
\begin{equation}\label{variation}
\begin{gathered}
 \xi=-\frac{n\cdot(\delta\gamma_+-\delta\gamma_-)}L,\qquad
 \zeta=\frac{\tau_+n\cdot\delta\gamma_--\tau_-n\cdot\delta\gamma_+}L,
 \qquad \zeta_w=\frac{\theta'P}{L}(w_+-w_-),\\
 C\psi=\frac{\pi}{n_2}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pv\,du,\qquad
 T\psi=\frac{\pi}{2n_2}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pv^2\,du,\qquad
 \delta V_K=\pi\int Yp,\\
 \delta F_V=C\psi-A\zeta-\delta\nu+(F_V'/\theta')\xi,\qquad
 \delta F_E=T\psi+d\delta\nu-\delta c+(F_E'/\theta')\xi-F_V\zeta.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Let $A_z$ be this linearization with the residual terms omitted, so
$D_zF=A_z+B_z[F]$, with $B_z[f]$ linear in $f_V,f_V',f_E'$.
The tangential equation is solved by $T_a-T_{-a}$ once
\begin{equation}\label{mean}
 \delta\nu\int c_V^{-1}\,dx
   =\int(C\psi-A\zeta_\psi-g_V)c_V^{-1}\,dx,
 \qquad c_V=-A\theta'P/L>0.
\end{equation}

For the normal equation, use $\theta$ as variable and put
$\partial=\partial_\theta$, $\kappa=d+d''$, $S=\tau_++\tau_-$,
and $K_jp=\int_{t_-}^{t_+}pv^j\,du$, where $t_\pm=x(\theta)\pm a$.
The moments $B_j=K_jp$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{moments}
\begin{aligned}
 B_0'&=p_+t_+'-p_-t_-',\\
 B_1''+B_1+\kappa B_0&=p_+\tau_+t_+'-p_-\tau_-t_-',\\
 B_2'''+4B_2'+6\kappa B_1'+2\kappa'B_1
   &=2(p_+\tau_+^2t_+'-p_-\tau_-^2t_-').
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Set $a_{\rm loc}=\kappa S/P$, $b_{\rm loc}=S/P$,
$e_{\rm loc}=-3\kappa/P-b_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}b_{\rm loc}$,
$M=b_{\rm loc}\partial+e_{\rm loc}$, and
$q=(S-\kappa')/P-e_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}e_{\rm loc}$.
Elimination gives $(\partial-a_{\rm loc})(B_0-MB_1)=qB_1+g_0$,
where $g_0=-(B_2'''+4B_2')/(2P)$.
The identity $(\partial-a_{\rm loc})\mathcal Q=q\mathcal P$ holds for
\begin{equation}\label{factorization}
\begin{gathered}
 \Delta=(q')^2+16q^2,\qquad H_q=q''-2a_{\rm loc}q'+16q,\qquad
 \varpi=H_qq'/\Delta,\\
 \upsilon=16+\varpi'+a_{\rm loc}'-a_{\rm loc}\varpi-a_{\rm loc}^2-16H_qq/\Delta,\\
 \mathcal P=\partial^2+\varpi\partial+\upsilon,\qquad
 \mathcal Q=q\partial+q(\varpi+a_{\rm loc})-q'.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
From \eqref{branch} and the endpoint equations,
$q=\varepsilon(192h/5)\sin4\theta+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Thus $\Delta=16(192h/5)^2\varepsilon^2+O(\varepsilon^3)$ on a complex
strip, and $\mathcal P=\partial^2+16+O(\varepsilon)$.
On antiperiodic functions both $\mathcal P$ and $\partial-a_{\rm loc}$ are
invertible; the latter has a periodic integrating factor.
With $\mathcal W=M\mathcal P+\mathcal Q$ and
$\chi_0=(\partial-a_{\rm loc})^{-1}g_0$, write
$B_1=\mathcal Pu$, $B_0=\mathcal Wu+\chi_0$. The reconstructed endpoints are
\begin{equation}\label{endpoints}
 p_\pm=A_\pm u+g_\pm,\quad
 A_\pm=\frac{(\partial^2+1)\mathcal P+
                   (\kappa-\tau_\mp\partial)\mathcal W}{Lt_\pm'},\quad
 g_\pm=\frac{\kappa\chi_0-\tau_\mp\chi_0'}{Lt_\pm'}.
\end{equation}
Pull back by $\partial_\theta=(\theta')^{-1}\partial_x$.
Endpoint agreement is the fourth-order difference equation
$\mathcal Lu=T_ag_--T_{-a}g_+$, where
$\mathcal L=T_{-a}A_+-T_aA_-$.
Parity and \eqref{moments} then give
\begin{equation}\label{reconstruction}
 B_0=K_0p,\qquad B_1=K_1p+C_*\sin\theta,\qquad
 B_2=K_2p-2C_*d\sin\theta.
\end{equation}
Consequently $B_2=(2\sin\theta/\pi)(g_E+\delta c)$ reconstructs
$T\psi+d\delta\nu=g_E+\delta c$ with $\delta\nu=-\pi C_*$.

Fix $\tau>\tau_*+1$ and a small $\gamma_0>0$, and impose
\begin{equation}\label{homogeneous}
 |2\sin(ma)|\ge\gamma_0(1+|m|)^{-\tau}
 \quad(0\ne m\in2\Z).
\end{equation}
Writing $-\mathcal L=B_+T_a-B_-T_{-a}$, its leading coefficients
$\beta_\pm$ satisfy $\beta_+(-x)=\beta_-(x)>0$.
Solve $(T_a-T_{-a})\log w_b=\log\beta_--\log\beta_+$ with zero mean
and put $e_b=\beta_+w_b(x+a)=\beta_-w_b(x-a)$.
For $D=-i\partial_x$ the balanced operator is
\begin{equation}\label{balanced}
 -e_b^{-1}\mathcal LM_{w_b}D^{-4}=P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a},\qquad
 P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^4p_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j}.
\end{equation}
Here $M_{w_b}$ is multiplication by $w_b$; the coefficients are
$\pi$-periodic, with $\bar p_{\pm,j}=(-1)^jp_{\pm,j}$ and
$p_{-,j}(x)=(-1)^jp_{+,j}(-x)$.
Lemma~\ref{fourier} gives a reduction
$(P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a})Q=E\mathcal D+\mathcal R$.
At the sphere its constant symbol and diagonal, for odd $k\ge3$, are
\begin{equation}\label{reference}
 M_+^*(k)=\frac{(k^2-16)(k^2-10/7+3ik/\sqrt7)}{k^4},\qquad
 d_k^*=-16i\sigma^3\frac{k^2-16}{k^4}C_{k-3}^{(3)}(h).
\end{equation}
Also $d_1^*=0$ and $\inf_{k\text{ odd}}|M_+^*(k)|>0$.
Thus the exceptional indices are $\mathcal F=\{-5,-1,1,5\}$;
write $\mathcal H=(2\Z+1)\setminus\mathcal F$ and $\ell_k=\log(2+|k|)$.
For Fourier matrices use the column norms
\begin{equation}\label{norms}
 \norm B_{\B_r}=\sup_k\sum_j e^{r|j-k|}|B_{jk}|,\qquad
 \norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}=\sup_k e^{c\ell_k^4}
                      \sum_j e^{r|j-k|}|\mathcal R_{jk}|.
\end{equation}
In particular
$\norm{B\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}
\le\norm B_{\B_r}\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}$.

\begin{proposition}\label{inverse}
Consider a family with first-order data \eqref{branch}, $\varepsilon\asymp t$,
and an $O(t^2)$ remainder in sufficiently many spatial derivatives.
Suppose \eqref{homogeneous} holds on its closed parameter set, the
normalizers satisfy $\norm{Q-I}_{\B_r}^{\Lip}+
\norm{E-I}_{\B_r}^{\Lip}\le1/4$, and
$\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp,\Lip}\le C_0t$.
If $|d_k|\ge\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $k\in\mathcal H$, with fixed
$\gamma>0$, then $A_z$ has a right inverse $N_z$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{inversebound}
 \norm{N_zg}_{r-C\delta}^{\Lip}\le K_t(\delta)\norm g_r^{\Lip},
 \qquad K_t(\delta)=t^{-p_0}e^{C\log^{p_0}(e/\delta)}.
\end{equation}
The same cost bounds changes of the geometric coefficients, normalizers,
diagonal symbols, and remainders, in their stated norms, divided by the
change of $z$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First solve the normal equation at prescribed density, modulo $1,f$,
with zero volume and amplitude. In the endpoint equation add a column
$\lambda X$, replace $g_E$ by $g_E+\delta c+\eta f$, and impose these
two constraints on the average reconstruction $p=(p^++p^-)/2$,
together with vanishing of the $\sin\theta$ coefficient $C_*$ of $B_1-K_1p$.
Integration by parts in \eqref{moments} gives
$\int X(p^+-p^-)=0$, forcing $\lambda=0$.

At the sphere
$A_\pm^*=(\partial^2+16)(\partial^2\pm3\partial/\sqrt7+10/7)/(2\sigma)$
and $\chi_0^*=(B_2''+4B_2)/(2\sigma^2)$.
The compatibility kernel is spanned by $\sin x,\sin5x$: the $X$ and $\eta$ columns
remove the two missing output modes, the amplitude fixes the latter
input mode, and the remaining volume and density constraints are
independent since $C_*=15u_1-(a_*-h\sigma)p_1$ and
$\partial_{\delta c}p_1=3/(2\pi\sigma^3)\ne0$; subscripts denote sine coefficients.
This finite block stays invertible near the branch. Its complementary
rows and columns have analytic $O(t)$ tails; for the density row this
follows by reversing the integrations in $K_1$.

After its elimination the complementary operator is
$\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}+\widehat{\mathcal R}$, with
$\norm{\widehat{\mathcal R}}_{r,c}^{\sharp}\le Ct$ on smaller strips.
The additional finite-rank term is $O(t^2)$ with exponential column decay.
Right multiplication by the diagonal inverse gives
\begin{equation}\label{neumann}
 (\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}+\widehat{\mathcal R})^{-1}
 =\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}
    (I+\widehat{\mathcal R}\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1})^{-1},\qquad
 \norm{\widehat{\mathcal R}\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}}_{\B_r}
 \le Ct/\gamma.
\end{equation}
The diagonal inverse costs $Ce^{C\log^3(e/\delta)}$.
Reconstruction therefore gives an inverse of
$\Pi T$, $\Pi g=g-\lambda_0(g)-\lambda_4(g)f$, on
$\{\delta V_K(\psi)=\lambda_4(\psi)=0\}$.
Its value norm is $O(1)$ across fixed positive strip gaps: in
\eqref{endpoints} the forcing passes through uniformly bounded
elliptic inverses, and $\Delta^{-1}$ appears only in bounded coefficients.

The volume row fixes dilation and the constant energy mode fixes
$\delta c$. Use the volume-zero amplitude direction
$f-\delta V_K(f)/\delta V_K(1)$ and write $\delta\nu=V_0\delta\rho$.
The critical and mean equations have the block
\begin{equation}\label{block}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)&
 \varepsilon\kappa_\rho+O(\varepsilon^2)\\
 -2\rho_1+O(\varepsilon)&1+O(\varepsilon)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Indeed the physical radial derivative in direction $f$ has critical
coefficient $c_4(h/5-h_1-b/5)=\beta_c$; changing to normal displacement
adds $T_hv$ and reparametrizes $T_hf=0$, so this coefficient is unchanged.
The density column is $V_0(d-\lambda_0d)=\varepsilon\kappa_\rho f+
O(\varepsilon^2)$, and \eqref{mean} uses
$\av f=1/5$, $(c_4-A_*h)/(5V_0)=2\rho_1$.
The bounded complementary inverse and $T_hf=0=\lambda_4T_h$ make its
correction to the critical row $O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Thus the determinant is $-\varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Finally \eqref{mean} permits the tangential solution under
\eqref{homogeneous}. These constructions and their difference estimates
give \eqref{inversebound}; the only amplitude losses are finite powers
of $t^{-1}$ from \eqref{factorization} and \eqref{block}.
\end{proof}

\section{Convergence}

Fix the divisor constants and positive initial and limiting widths.
Take $\gamma>0$ so that $|d_k^*|\ge4\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ on
$\mathcal H$, using Lemma~\ref{arithmetic}.
Choose $\mu>32$, $N>3p_0+\mu+4$, and $z_0=z^{[N]}$.
On fixed inner strips its normalized coefficients have bounded
unweighted parameter seminorms: the powers of $a-a_*$ cancel in
\eqref{factorization}. Initially the normalizers are $I+O(t)$ and
the raw remainder is $O(t)$.
Let $r_{j+1}=r_j-\delta_j\downarrow r_\infty>0$, with
$\delta_j=d_0(j+1)^{-2}$, and put $\Gamma_j=\gamma(1+2^{-j})$.
Let $G_0\subset I_t$ be the set satisfying \eqref{homogeneous} and
$|d_{0,k}|\ge2\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $k\in\mathcal H$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{iteration}
 v_j=-N_{z_j}F(z_j,a),\quad z_{j+1}=z_j+v_j,\qquad
 G_{j+1}=\{a\in G_j:|d_{j+1,k}(a)|\ge\Gamma_{j+1}e^{-\ell_k^3},\ k\in\mathcal H\}.
\end{equation}
All objects at stage $j+1$ are first constructed on $G_j$.
For $e_j=\norm{F(z_j,\cdot)}_{r_j}^{\Lip}$ and
$\Lambda=\log(1/t)$, Taylor's theorem and $DF=A_z+B_z[F]$ give
\begin{equation}\label{recurrence}
 e_{j+1}\le K_je_j^2,\qquad
 \norm{v_j}_{r_j-\delta_j/2}^{\Lip}\le K_je_j,\qquad
 \log K_j\le p_0\Lambda+C(1+\log(j+2))^{p_0}.
\end{equation}
Allocate fixed fractions of $\delta_j$ to each operation and enlarge
$K_j$ to cover the operator increments in Proposition~\ref{inverse}.
Since $\sum_j2^{-j-1}\log K_j\le p_0\Lambda+C$, the recurrence gives
$e_j\le t^{(N-p_0-1)2^j}$ and $K_j^2e_j\le t^{\mu2^j}$.
The width-independent construction in Lemma~\ref{fourier} therefore

\section{Fourier reduction}

\begin{lemma}\label{fourier}
Let $L_0=P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a}$ with
$P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^Jp_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j}$, $J$ fixed, and bounded
$\pi$-periodic coefficients satisfying the symmetries of \eqref{balanced}.
Assume \eqref{homogeneous}. For constant reference coefficients $p^*$
put $\eta=\max_{\pm,j}\norm{p_{\pm,j}-p_{\pm,j}^*}_r$.
There are width-independent operators satisfying
$L_0Q=E\mathcal D+\mathcal R$, with
$\mathcal D=M_+(D)T_a-M_-(D)T_{-a}$, such that, for $r'=r-C\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{fourierbound}
 \norm{Q-I}_{\B_{r'}}+\norm{E-I}_{\B_{r'}}+
 \sup_k|k|\sum_\pm|M_\pm(k)-P_\pm^*(k)|+
 \norm{\mathcal R}_{r',c}^{\sharp}
 \le C\eta e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)}.
\end{equation}
The same bound holds for input differences and in weighted Lipschitz
norms, including differences of families on a common closed parameter set.
Moreover $M_-=\overline{M_+}$; near a nonvanishing reference,
$d_k=2iA_k\sin(ka+\phi_k)$ with $A_k$ bounded above and below, and
bounded unweighted input seminorms on a fixed strip imply
$\Lip\phi_k\le C/|k|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use the formal product
$p\#q=\sum_{\alpha\ge0}(\partial_k^\alpha p)D_x^\alpha q/\alpha!$.
Seek $Q=1+\sum q_nk^{-n}$, $E=1+\sum e_nk^{-n}$ and
$M_\pm=1+\sum m_{\pm,n}k^{-n}$, with $q_n,e_n$ of mean zero.
If $f_{\pm,n}$ is the coefficient of $k^{-n}$ in
$P_\pm\#Q_{<n}(x\pm a,k)-E_{<n}M_{\pm,<n}$, the recursion is
\begin{equation}\label{symbolrecursion}
 m_{\pm,n}=\av{f_{\pm,n}},\quad
 (T_a-T_{-a})q_n=-\Pi_0(f_{+,n}-f_{-,n}),\quad
 e_n=T_aq_n+f_{+,n}-m_{+,n},
\end{equation}
where $\Pi_0$ removes the mean.
Each term of grade $n$ has $O(n)$ operations and at most $n$ derivatives.
Allocate $\delta/(Cn)$ to each operation along a branch of the recursion;
Cauchy's estimate and \eqref{homogeneous} give, for fixed $B,\varkappa$,
\begin{equation}\label{factorial}
 \norm{q_n}_{r-\delta}+\norm{e_n}_{r-\delta}+
 \sum_\pm|m_{\pm,n}-p_{\pm,n}^*|
 \le\eta(C\delta^{-B})^n(n!)^\varkappa.
\end{equation}
The factorial absorbs grade allocations and powers of $n$.
Telescoping marks an input difference; parameter differences cost one
derivative for translations and two homogeneous divisors for reciprocals.
This proves the same estimate for differences of families.

In column $k$ truncate at $N(k)=\lfloor\ell_k^3\rfloor$, retaining the
reference polynomial $P_\pm^*$ exactly in $M_\pm$.
For $A\ge1$, factorial estimates give
$\sum_{n=1}^{2N+J}A^n(n!)^\varkappa|k|^{-n}\le
|k|^{-1}e^{C(1+\log A)^4}$ and its tail after $N$ is at most
$e^{C(1+\log A)^4-c\ell_k^4}$.

To control the exact product, split its Fourier shifts at
$|\nu|=|k|/2$. Below this threshold, Taylor expansion of
$(k+\nu)^{-j}$ through total grade $N$ reproduces the formal product;
the remainder is bounded by \eqref{factorial} and the factorial tail.
Above it, $k+\nu$ is odd and nonzero, and a further strip margin gives
$e^{-\delta|k|/4}\le e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)-c\ell_k^4}$.
The product $EM_\pm$ is multiplication of column symbols, with omitted
grades at most $2N+J$. These estimates prove \eqref{fourierbound},
also for exact differences; factors $|k|$ from translated parameter
differences are absorbed by decreasing $c$ once.
The recursion preserves reality and reflection, hence
$M_- =\overline{M_+}$.
Finally $\Lip M_+(k)\le C/|k|$ on a fixed strip, and the logarithm
of $M_+/P_+^*$ near one gives the phase bound.
\end{proof}

in a direction $n$ when the cap of volume $\rho\vol K$ cut off normal to $n$

Ryabogin constructed nonspherical examples floating in every orientation
at density $1/2$ \cite{Ryabogin22}; central symmetry at that density forces

The map taking the lower endpoint of a prescribed-volume chord to its

reflection and commutes with translation by $\pi$.
Its normalized formal conjugacy to translation by $2a(\varepsilon)$ is

Differentiating the endpoint equation

For a variation write $\delta\gamma=\psi N+w\gamma'$, where
$s=|\gamma'|$, $N=(Y',-X')/s$, $\psi$ is even and $\pi$-periodic,
and $w$ is odd and $\pi$-periodic. Set
$p=2Ys\psi$, $\tau_\pm=e\cdot\gamma_\pm-d_\theta$,
$P=\tau_+\tau_-<0$ and $\zeta=\delta d-d_\theta\delta\theta$.
Varying $n\cdot\gamma_\pm=d$ gives
$\zeta=(\tau_+n\cdot\delta\gamma_--\tau_-n\cdot\delta\gamma_+)/L$;
its tangential part is $\zeta_w=(\theta'P/L)(T_a-T_{-a})w$.
Shape differentiation at a fixed cutting plane gives
\begin{equation}\label{variation}
 C\psi=\frac{\pi}{n_2}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pv\,du,\qquad
 T\psi=\frac{\pi}{2n_2}\int_{x-a}^{x+a}pv^2\,du.
\end{equation}
With $c_V=-A\theta'P/L>0$, define the approximate linearization by
\begin{equation}\label{linearization}
\begin{aligned}
 (A_z\delta z)_V&=C\psi-A\zeta_\psi+c_V(T_a-T_{-a})w-\delta\nu,\\
 (A_z\delta z)_E&=T\psi+d\delta\nu-\delta c,\qquad
 (A_z\delta z)_0=\delta V_K(\psi)=\pi\int_0^{2\pi}Yp\,du.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The omitted terms are $(F_V'/\theta')\delta\theta$ and
$(F_E'/\theta')\delta\theta-F_V\zeta$ in the first two rows. Thus
$D_zF=A_z+B_z[F]$, with $B_z[f]$ linear in $f_V,f_V',f_E'$.
The normal equation determines the shape; the tangential equation determines
its parametrization. They are coupled through $\delta\nu$.
For $A_z\delta z=g$, the tangential equation is solvable precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{mean}
 \delta\nu\int c_V^{-1}\,dx
   =\int(C\psi-A\zeta_\psi-g_V)c_V^{-1}\,dx,
\end{equation}
provided the nonzero even Fourier divisors $2\sin(ma)$ are bounded below.

To solve the normal equation, we replace the cap integral by agreement
of two reconstructed endpoint values. Use $\theta$ as variable and put
$\partial=\partial_\theta$, $\kappa=d+d''$, $S=\tau_++\tau_-$,
and $K_jp=\int_{t_-}^{t_+}pv^j\,du$, where $t_\pm=x(\theta)\pm a$.
The moments $B_j=K_jp$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{moments}
\begin{aligned}
 B_0'&=p_+t_+'-p_-t_-',\\
 B_1''+B_1+\kappa B_0&=p_+\tau_+t_+'-p_-\tau_-t_-',\\
 B_2'''+4B_2'+6\kappa B_1'+2\kappa'B_1
   &=2(p_+\tau_+^2t_+'-p_-\tau_-^2t_-').
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Set $a_{\rm loc}=\kappa S/P$, $b_{\rm loc}=S/P$,
$e_{\rm loc}=-3\kappa/P-b_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}b_{\rm loc}$,
$M=b_{\rm loc}\partial+e_{\rm loc}$, and
$q=(S-\kappa')/P-e_{\rm loc}'+a_{\rm loc}e_{\rm loc}$.
Elimination gives $(\partial-a_{\rm loc})(B_0-MB_1)=qB_1+g_0$,
where $g_0=-(B_2'''+4B_2')/(2P)$.
The identity $(\partial-a_{\rm loc})\mathcal Q=q\mathcal P$ holds for
\begin{equation}\label{factorization}
\begin{gathered}
 \Delta=(q')^2+16q^2,\qquad H_q=q''-2a_{\rm loc}q'+16q,\qquad
 \varpi=H_qq'/\Delta,\\
 \upsilon=16+\varpi'+a_{\rm loc}'-a_{\rm loc}\varpi-a_{\rm loc}^2-16H_qq/\Delta,\\
 \mathcal P=\partial^2+\varpi\partial+\upsilon,\qquad
 \mathcal Q=q\partial+q(\varpi+a_{\rm loc})-q'.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
From \eqref{branch} and the endpoint equations,
$q=\varepsilon(192h/5)\sin4\theta+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Thus $\Delta=16(192h/5)^2\varepsilon^2+O(\varepsilon^3)$ on a complex
strip, and $\mathcal P=\partial^2+16+O(\varepsilon)$.
On antiperiodic functions both $\mathcal P$ and $\partial-a_{\rm loc}$ are
invertible; $a_{\rm loc}$ is odd and $\pi$-periodic, so the latter
has a periodic integrating factor.
With $\mathcal W=M\mathcal P+\mathcal Q$ and
$\chi_0=(\partial-a_{\rm loc})^{-1}g_0$, write
$B_1=\mathcal Pu$, $B_0=\mathcal Wu+\chi_0$, with $u$ odd and antiperiodic.
The reconstructed endpoints are
\begin{equation}\label{endpoints}
 p_\pm=A_\pm u+g_\pm,\quad
 A_\pm=\frac{(\partial^2+1)\mathcal P+
                   (\kappa-\tau_\mp\partial)\mathcal W}{Lt_\pm'},\quad
 g_\pm=\frac{\kappa\chi_0-\tau_\mp\chi_0'}{Lt_\pm'}.
\end{equation}
Pull back by $\partial_\theta=(\theta')^{-1}\partial_x$.
Endpoint agreement is the fourth-order difference equation
$\mathcal Lu=T_ag_--T_{-a}g_+$, where
$\mathcal L=T_{-a}A_+-T_aA_-$; both sides are even and antiperiodic.
Subtracting the moments $K_jp$ from the reconstructed triple gives
$E_0'=0$ and $E_1''+E_1=0$, hence $E_0=0$ and
$E_1=C_*\sin\theta$ by odd antiperiodicity.
Since $(\partial^3+4\partial)(d\sin\theta)=
\kappa'\sin\theta+3\kappa\cos\theta$, the third identity gives
$(\partial^3+4\partial)(E_2+2C_*d\sin\theta)=0$.
Its kernel has no antiperiodic function, so
\begin{equation}\label{reconstruction}
 B_0=K_0p,\qquad B_1=K_1p+C_*\sin\theta,\qquad
 B_2=K_2p-2C_*d\sin\theta.
\end{equation}
Consequently $B_2=(2\sin\theta/\pi)(g_E+\delta c)$ reconstructs
$T\psi+d\delta\nu=g_E+\delta c$ with $\delta\nu=-\pi C_*$.

\section{The right inverse}

Fix $\tau>\tau_*+1$ and a small $\gamma_0>0$, and impose
\begin{equation}\label{homogeneous}
 |2\sin(ma)|\ge\gamma_0(1+|m|)^{-\tau}
 \quad(0\ne m\in2\Z).
\end{equation}
Writing $-\mathcal L=B_+T_a-B_-T_{-a}$, its leading coefficients
$\beta_\pm$ satisfy $\beta_+(-x)=\beta_-(x)>0$.
Solve $(T_a-T_{-a})\log w_b=\log\beta_--\log\beta_+$ with zero mean
and put $e_b=\beta_+w_b(x+a)=\beta_-w_b(x-a)$; both are even
and $\pi$-periodic.
For $D=-i\partial_x$ the balanced operator is
\begin{equation}\label{balanced}
 -e_b^{-1}\mathcal LM_{w_b}D^{-4}=P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a},\qquad
 P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^4p_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j}.
\end{equation}
Here $M_{w_b}$ is multiplication by $w_b$; the coefficients are
$\pi$-periodic, with $\bar p_{\pm,j}=(-1)^jp_{\pm,j}$ and
$p_{-,j}(x)=(-1)^jp_{+,j}(-x)$.
Lemma~\ref{fourier} gives a reduction
$(P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a})Q=E\mathcal D+\mathcal R$, where
$d_k=M_+(k)e^{ika}-M_-(k)e^{-ika}$ are the multipliers of $\mathcal D$.
At the sphere its constant symbol and diagonal, for odd $k\ge3$, are
\begin{equation}\label{reference}
 M_+^*(k)=\frac{(k^2-16)(k^2-10/7+3ik/\sqrt7)}{k^4},\qquad
 d_k^*=-16i\sigma^3\frac{k^2-16}{k^4}C_{k-3}^{(3)}(h).
\end{equation}
Also $d_1^*=0$ and $\inf_{k\text{ odd}}|M_+^*(k)|>0$.
Thus the exceptional indices are $\mathcal F=\{-5,-1,1,5\}$;
write $\mathcal H=(2\Z+1)\setminus\mathcal F$ and $\ell_k=\log(2+|k|)$.
For Fourier matrices use the column norms
\begin{equation}\label{norms}
 \norm B_{\B_r}=\sup_k\sum_j e^{r|j-k|}|B_{jk}|,\qquad
 \norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}=\sup_k e^{c\ell_k^4}
                      \sum_j e^{r|j-k|}|\mathcal R_{jk}|.
\end{equation}
In particular $\norm{B\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}
\le\norm B_{\B_r}\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp}$.

\begin{proposition}\label{inverse}
Let $z(a)$ be a family on a closed $G\subset I_t$ with
$\norm{z-z^{[N]}}_{r,12}^{\Lip}\le Ct^2$, taking the scalar components
in their absolute-value norms.
Let $\widehat{\mathcal R}$ be the complementary remainder after
multiplication by $E^{-1}$ and elimination of the constrained finite block below.
Suppose \eqref{homogeneous} holds on $G$, the normalizers satisfy
$\norm{Q-I}_{\B_r}^{\Lip}+\norm{E-I}_{\B_r}^{\Lip}\le1/4$, and
$\norm{\mathcal R}_{r,c}^{\sharp,\Lip}+
\norm{\widehat{\mathcal R}}_{r,c}^{\sharp,\Lip}\le C_0t$.
If $|d_k|\ge\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $k\in\mathcal H$, with fixed
$\gamma>0$, then $A_z$ has a right inverse on triples
$g=(g_V,g_E,g_0)$ with $g_V,g_E$ even and $\pi$-periodic and $g_0\in\R$.
It returns variations of the prescribed parity and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{inversebound}
 \norm{N_zg}_{r-C\delta}^{\Lip}\le K_t(\delta)\norm g_r^{\Lip},
 \qquad K_t(\delta)=t^{-p_0}e^{C\log^{p_0}(e/\delta)}.
\end{equation}
On a common parameter set, changing $z$ by $\widetilde z-z$ changes
the geometric coefficients, normalizers, diagonal symbols, and both remainders
by at most $K_t(\delta)\norm{\widetilde z-z}_r^{\Lip}$ on the smaller
strip, in their respective norms. The exponent $p_0$ is independent of $N$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\emph{The constrained normal inverse.}
First solve with $\delta\nu=0$, modulo $1,f$,
with zero volume and amplitude. In the endpoint equation add a column
$\lambda X$, take $B_2=(2\sin\theta/\pi)(g_E+\delta c+\eta f)$, and impose these
two constraints on $p=(p^++p^-)/2$, where
$p^\pm=T_{\mp a}(A_\pm u+g_\pm)$, together with vanishing of the
$\sin\theta$ coefficient $C_*$ of $B_1-K_1p$.
These conditions are defined before endpoint agreement.
Writing $b_1=B_1''+B_1+\kappa B_0$, the endpoint formulas give
\[
 \int X(p^+-p^-)\,dx
 =\int[-\sin\theta\,b_1+(d\cos\theta-d'\sin\theta)B_0']\,d\theta=0.
\]
The last equality is integration by parts, since
$(d\cos\theta-d'\sin\theta)'=-\kappa\sin\theta$.
Thus $\lambda\int X^2=0$, and the reconstructed endpoints agree.

At the sphere
$A_\pm^*=(\partial^2+16)(\partial^2\pm3\partial/\sqrt7+10/7)/(2\sigma)$
and $\chi_0^*=(B_2''+4B_2)/(2\sigma^2)$.
The compatibility kernel is spanned by $\sin x,\sin5x$: the $X$ and $\eta$ columns
remove the two missing output modes, the amplitude fixes the latter
input mode, and the remaining volume and density constraints are
independent since $C_*=15u_1-(a_*-h\sigma)p_1$ and
$\partial_{\delta c}p_1=3/(2\pi\sigma^3)\ne0$; subscripts denote sine coefficients.
This finite block stays invertible near the branch. Its complementary
rows and columns have analytic $O(t)$ tails; for the density row this
follows by reversing the integrations in $K_1$.

First multiply the balanced equation by $E^{-1}$, then eliminate this
uniformly invertible finite block. The complementary operator is
$\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}+\widehat{\mathcal R}$, whose raw norm is bounded
by hypothesis. Its additional finite-rank term is $O(t^2)$ with
exponential column decay; its construction does not use
$\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}$.
Right multiplication by the diagonal inverse gives
\begin{equation}\label{neumann}
 (\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}+\widehat{\mathcal R})^{-1}
 =\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}
    (I+\widehat{\mathcal R}\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1})^{-1},\qquad
 \norm{\widehat{\mathcal R}\mathcal D_{\mathcal H}^{-1}}_{\B_r}
 \le Ct/\gamma.
\end{equation}
The diagonal inverse costs $Ce^{C\log^3(e/\delta)}$.
Reconstruction therefore gives an inverse of
$\Pi T$, $\Pi g=g-\lambda_0(g)-\lambda_4(g)f$, on
$\{\delta V_K(\psi)=\lambda_4(\psi)=0\}$.
Its value norm is $O(1)$ across fixed positive strip gaps: in
\eqref{endpoints} the forcing passes through uniformly bounded
elliptic inverses, and $\Delta^{-1}$ appears only in bounded coefficients.

\emph{The amplitude and density.}
The volume row fixes dilation and the constant energy mode fixes
$\delta c$. Use the volume-zero amplitude direction
$f-\delta V_K(f)/\delta V_K(1)$ and write $\delta\nu=V_0\delta\rho$.
The critical and mean equations have the block
\begin{equation}\label{block}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)&
 \varepsilon\kappa_\rho+O(\varepsilon^2)\\
 -2\rho_1+O(\varepsilon)&1+O(\varepsilon)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Indeed the physical radial derivative in direction $f$ has critical
coefficient $c_4(h/5-h_1-b/5)=\beta_c$; changing to normal displacement
adds $T_hv$ and reparametrizes $T_hf=0$, so this coefficient is unchanged.
The density column is $V_0(d-\lambda_0d)=\varepsilon\kappa_\rho f+
O(\varepsilon^2)$, and \eqref{mean} uses
$\av f=1/5$, $(c_4-A_*h)/(5V_0)=2\rho_1$.
The bounded complementary inverse and $T_hf=0=\lambda_4T_h$ make its
correction to the critical row $O(\varepsilon^2)$.
Thus the determinant is $-\varepsilon\beta_c+O(\varepsilon^2)$.

\emph{The parametrization.}
Finally \eqref{mean} permits the tangential solution under
\eqref{homogeneous}. These constructions and their difference estimates
give \eqref{inversebound}; the only amplitude losses are finite powers
of $t^{-1}$ from \eqref{factorization} and \eqref{block}.
\end{proof}

\section{Convergence}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{main}]

Fix the divisor constants and positive initial and limiting widths.
Take $\gamma>0$ so that $|d_k^*|\ge4\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ on
$\mathcal H$, using Lemma~\ref{arithmetic}.
Choose $\mu>32$, $N>3p_0+\mu+4$, and $z_0=z^{[N]}$.
On fixed inner strips its normalized coefficients have bounded
unweighted parameter seminorms: the powers of $a-a_*$ cancel in
\eqref{factorization}. On the closed subset satisfying
\eqref{homogeneous}, construct the normalizers across a fixed initial
strip gap. They are $I+O(t)$, and both raw remainders are $O(t)$.
Let $r_{j+1}=r_j-\delta_j\downarrow r_\infty>0$, with
$\delta_j=d_0(j+1)^{-2}$, and put $\Gamma_j=\gamma(1+2^{-j})$.
Let $G_0\subset I_t$ be the set satisfying \eqref{homogeneous} and
$|d_{0,k}|\ge2\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $k\in\mathcal H$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{iteration}
 v_j=-N_{z_j}F(z_j,a),\quad z_{j+1}=z_j+v_j,\qquad
 G_{j+1}=\{a\in G_j:|d_{j+1,k}(a)|\ge
 \Gamma_{j+1}e^{-\ell_k^3},\ k\in\mathcal H\}.
\end{equation}
All objects at stage $j+1$ are first constructed on $G_j$.

\emph{Newton estimates.}
For $e_j=\norm{F(z_j,\cdot)}_{r_j}^{\Lip}$ and
$\Lambda=\log(1/t)$, Taylor's theorem and $DF=A_z+B_z[F]$ give
\begin{equation}\label{recurrence}
 e_{j+1}\le K_je_j^2,\qquad \norm{v_j}_{r_j-\delta_j/2}^{\Lip}\le K_je_j,\qquad
 \log K_j\le p_0\Lambda+C(1+\log(j+2))^{p_0}.
\end{equation}
Allocate fixed fractions of $\delta_j$ to each operation, including
the twelve Cauchy derivatives, and enlarge $K_j$ to cover the
coefficient and operator increments in Proposition~\ref{inverse}.
Since $\sum_j2^{-j-1}\log K_j\le p_0\Lambda+C$, the recurrence gives
$e_j\le t^{(N-p_0-1)2^j}$ and $K_j^2e_j\le t^{\mu2^j}$.
In particular $\norm{v_j}_{r_{j+1},12}^{\Lip}\le t^{\mu2^j}$.
The width-independent construction in Lemma~\ref{fourier} has summable
increments in $\B_r$ and the raw $\sharp$ norm, estimating each increment
across the new margin and restricting the previous operators, for both
$\mathcal R$ and $\widehat{\mathcal R}$.
The product inequality following \eqref{norms} controls $E^{-1}\mathcal R$;
the finite-rank terms cost at most $e^{C\log^4(e/\delta_j)}$ across the
new margin, already included in $K_j$.
Thus the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{inverse} persist.
On two fixed strips strictly inside $r_\infty$, the normalized coefficient
seminorms also stay bounded: divide the weighted increment bounds by $t$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{fourier} across their fixed gap. Width independence gives
the same diagonal symbols as in the iteration.
In particular
\begin{equation}\label{phases}
 \begin{gathered}
 d_{j,k}=2iA_{j,k}\sin(ka+\phi_{j,k}),\qquad 0<A_-\le A_{j,k}\le A_+,\\
 \Lip\phi_{j,k}\le C/|k|,\qquad
 |d_{j+1,k}-d_{j,k}|\le t^{\mu2^j}(1+|k|)^{p_0}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}

\emph{Parameter exclusions.}
For large $|k|$, the phase map on a closed subset of $I_t$ has lower
Lipschitz bound $|k|/2$; its range meets $O(t|k|+1)$ intervals of radius
$O(\gamma e^{-\ell_k^3})$ about $\pi\Z$. Each inverse image has diameter
$O(\gamma |k|^{-1}e^{-\ell_k^3})$, so
\begin{equation}\label{measure}
 |\{a\in G:|d_{j,k}(a)|<\Gamma e^{-\ell_k^3}\}|
 \le C\gamma(t+|k|^{-1})e^{-\ell_k^3},\qquad \gamma\le\Gamma\le2\gamma.
\end{equation}
The reference arithmetic protects the homogeneous modes through
$M_t\asymp t^{-1/(\tau_*+1)}$; their remaining exclusions have measure
$O(tM_t^{1-\tau}+M_t^{-\tau})=o(t)$.
Likewise $|d_{0,k}-d_k^*|\le Ct(1+|k|)^{p_0}$ protects the complementary
modes through $K_t=\lfloor e^{\kappa_0\sqrt\Lambda}\rfloor$ for small
fixed $\kappa_0>0$. Summing \eqref{measure} beyond $K_t$ gives $o(t)$,
so $|I_t\setminus G_0|=o(t)$.

At stage $j$ set $s_j=\mu2^j\Lambda$ and
$N_j=\lfloor e^{(s_j/4)^{1/3}}\rfloor$.
The increment in \eqref{phases} is smaller than the threshold slack
$\gamma2^{-j-1}e^{-\ell_k^3}$ for $|k|\le N_j$.
For larger modes, \eqref{measure} gives
$|G_j\setminus G_{j+1}|\le Ce^{-s_j/16}$ by integral comparison.
Their sum is $O(t^{\mu/16})=o(t)$. Inductively, the initial loss and
every finite partial sum are smaller than $|I_t|/2$ for small $t$,
so $G_j$ is nonempty before step $j$ is performed and
$|I_t\setminus\bigcap_jG_j|=o(t)$.

On $G_t=\bigcap_jG_j$ the iterates converge on a positive strip to a
solution of \eqref{F}, with total correction $O(t^\mu)$.
Thus \eqref{branch} persists and yields \eqref{asymptotics} upon using
the actual degree-four radial coefficient.
At an axis pole, symmetry writes $Y=u\alpha(u^2)$,
$X=X_0+u^2\beta(u^2)$ with $\alpha(0)\ne0$; analytic inversion gives
$X=\chi(Y^2)$, so revolution preserves analyticity there.
The boundary is $C^2$-close to the sphere and strictly convex, while
its nonzero degree-four coefficient excludes a ball.
The normal angle and revolution cover all directions, and constant
cap volume and energy give equilibrium in every orientation.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{fourier}
On antiperiodic functions let $L_0=P_+T_a-P_-T_{-a}$ with
$P_\pm=I+\sum_{j=1}^Jp_{\pm,j}(x)D^{-j}$, $J$ fixed, and bounded
$\pi$-periodic coefficients satisfying the symmetries of \eqref{balanced}.
Assume \eqref{homogeneous}. For constant reference coefficients $p^*$
put $P_\pm^*(k)=1+\sum_{j=1}^Jp_{\pm,j}^*k^{-j}$ and
$\eta=\max_{\pm,j}\norm{p_{\pm,j}-p_{\pm,j}^*}_r\le1$, setting
$p_{\pm,n}^*=0$ for $n>J$.
There are width-independent operators satisfying
$L_0Q=E\mathcal D+\mathcal R$, with
$\mathcal D=M_+(D)T_a-M_-(D)T_{-a}$, such that, for $r'=r-C\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{fourierbound}
 \norm{Q-I}_{\B_{r'}}+\norm{E-I}_{\B_{r'}}+
 \sup_k|k|\sum_\pm|M_\pm(k)-P_\pm^*(k)|+
 \norm{\mathcal R}_{r',c}^{\sharp}
 \le C\eta e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)}.
\end{equation}
The same bound holds for input differences and in weighted Lipschitz
norms, including differences of families on a common closed parameter set.
Moreover $M_-=\overline{M_+}$; near a nonvanishing reference,
$d_k=2iA_k\sin(ka+\phi_k)$ with $A_k$ bounded above and below, and
bounded unweighted input seminorms on a fixed strip imply
$\Lip\phi_k\le C/|k|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the formal product
$p\#q=\sum_{\alpha\ge0}(\partial_k^\alpha p)D_x^\alpha q/\alpha!$.
Seek $Q=1+\sum q_nk^{-n}$, $E=1+\sum e_nk^{-n}$ and
$M_\pm=1+\sum m_{\pm,n}k^{-n}$, with $q_n,e_n$ of mean zero.
If $f_{\pm,n}$ is the coefficient of $k^{-n}$ in
$P_\pm\#Q_{<n}(x\pm a,k)-E_{<n}M_{\pm,<n}$, the recursion is
\begin{equation}\label{symbolrecursion}
 m_{\pm,n}=\av{f_{\pm,n}},\quad
 (T_a-T_{-a})q_n=-\Pi_0(f_{+,n}-f_{-,n}),\quad
 e_n=T_aq_n+f_{+,n}-m_{+,n},
\end{equation}
where $\Pi_0$ removes the mean.
At the reference $q_n=e_n=0$ and $m_{\pm,n}=p_{\pm,n}^*$.
The recursion preserves
$\overline{q_n}=q_n(-x)=(-1)^nq_n$, the same identities for $e_n$, and
$m_{-,n}=\overline{m_{+,n}}=(-1)^nm_{+,n}$.
Each recursive product tree of grade $n$ has at most $Cn$ vertices,
$n$ derivatives, and $n$ homogeneous inversions.
Allocate $\delta/(Cn)$ to each vertex along a branch;
Cauchy's estimate and \eqref{homogeneous} give, for fixed $B,\varkappa$,
\begin{equation}\label{factorial}
 \norm{q_n}_{r-\delta}+\norm{e_n}_{r-\delta}+
 \sum_\pm|m_{\pm,n}-p_{\pm,n}^*|
 \le\eta(C\delta^{-B})^n(n!)^\varkappa.
\end{equation}
The factorial absorbs grade allocations and powers of $n$.
Telescoping marks an input difference; parameter differences cost one
derivative for translations and two homogeneous divisors for reciprocals.
This proves the same estimate for differences of families.

In column $k$ truncate $Q,E$ at $N(k)=\lfloor\ell_k^3\rfloor$ and set
$M_\pm(k)=P_\pm^*(k)+\sum_{n\le N(k)}(m_{\pm,n}-p_{\pm,n}^*)k^{-n}$,
retaining the reference polynomial exactly.
For $A\ge1$, factorial estimates give
$\sum_{n=1}^{2N+J}A^n(n!)^\varkappa|k|^{-n}\le

$e^{C(1+\log A)^4-c\ell_k^4}$.

Define $\mathcal R=L_0Q-E\mathcal D$ by the exact product and split its Fourier shifts at
$|\nu|=|k|/2$. Below this threshold, Taylor expansion of
$(k+\nu)^{-j}$ through total grade $N$ reproduces the formal product;
the remainder is bounded by \eqref{factorial} and the factorial tail,
using Cauchy's inequality for its powers of $\nu$ with the same grade allocation.
Above it, $k+\nu$ is odd and nonzero, and a further strip margin gives
$e^{-\delta|k|/4}\le e^{C\log^4(e/\delta)-c\ell_k^4}$.
The product $EM_\pm$ is multiplication of column symbols, with omitted
grades at most $2N+J$. Every remaining term contains a perturbation
factor, since the reference cancels identically.
These estimates prove \eqref{fourierbound},
